levels.title: Level 1 — Foundations
levels.blurb: From first block to a complete game a child designs themselves. Motion, looks, events, loops, sensing, conditionals and variables.

levels.title: Level 2 — Logic, Data and Game Engineering
levels.blurb: Real programming: operators, lists, broadcasts, clones, custom blocks, physics, pen, music, debugging and publishing.

L1S1.title: Welcome to Scratch

blockRefs.what: Starts the script when the green flag is pressed.
blockRefs.tip: Every project needs one — it's how everything begins.

explain: Scratch is made of four areas. The **stage** is the screen where your project happens. The **sprite list** below it holds every character. The **block palette** on the left holds the instructions, sorted by colour. The **code area** in the middle is where you build.

Every sprite carries its own code, its own costumes and its own sounds. That is important: if you click the wrong sprite, you will write code in the wrong place. Professional programmers call this 'scope' — where a piece of code belongs.
Blocks only run when something tells them to. Clicking a block runs it once. A hat block on top makes it run whenever an event happens. Nothing in Scratch happens by accident.

examples.title: Your first script
examples.code:
when green flag clicked
say [Hello!] for 2 seconds
move 50 steps
examples.note: The hat block listens for the flag. Everything below runs in order.

examples.title: Testing one block
examples.code: move 10 steps
examples.note: Click a block on its own to run it immediately — the fastest way to find out what it does.

deep.why: Knowing where code lives is the difference between fixing a bug in ten seconds and hunting for it for ten minutes.
deep.real: A TV remote only works when you press a button — the press is the event, the channel change is the code.
extend: Add a second sprite and give it its own code
Try the same script on the Stage and see what changes
Rename sprites so you can tell them apart

vocab: Sprite — a character or object you can give code to.
Stage — the screen where your project happens.
Script — a stack of blocks joined together.
Palette — the coloured menu where blocks live.
objectives: I can name the stage, the sprite list and the block palette.
I can drag a block into the code area and run it.
I can start a project with the green flag.
L1S1.hook: Show the child a finished game for 30 seconds and say: "By the end of today YOU will have made something that runs like this. Ready?"
teach: Share your screen with a brand-new Scratch project. Point at three places only: the Stage (top right), the Sprite list (under it), the Block palette (left). Name each one and have the child repeat it back.
Drag a `move 10 steps` block into the code area and click it. Say: "Blocks do nothing until something runs them — clicking is one way."
Snap `when green flag clicked` on top and run it with the flag. Say: "Now the flag runs it. This is how every project starts."
Hand over: ask the child to share their screen and do the same three steps themselves.
watch: Child clicks the flag but nothing happens → the script has no hat block; check `when green flag clicked` is on top.
Blocks are dropped near each other but not snapped → zoom in and show the white snap line as blocks join.
Child edits the Stage instead of the sprite → point out the highlighted sprite thumbnail.
ask: Where does a sprite's code live? → In the code area, when that sprite is selected.
What does the green flag do? → Runs every `when green flag clicked` script.
What is a sprite? → A character or object you can program.
L1S1.support: Do it hand-over-hand: you drag, they click run. Reduce to one block and one goal — make the cat move.
L1S1.stretch: Ask them to add a second block so the cat moves AND turns, then predict what will happen before running it.

rubric.emerging: Needs help to find the palette and drag a block.
rubric.secure: Drags, snaps and runs a two-block script independently.
rubric.mastered: Explains stage/sprite/script in their own words and helps someone else find them.

L1S1.homework: Open Scratch at home and make the cat say your name.

runSheet.note: Also ask one recall question from last session.

runSheet.note: Ask the child to PREDICT before you run anything.

runSheet.note: Hands off the mouse — prompt with questions.

L1S2.title: Steps in order

blockRefs.what: Moves the sprite forwards in the direction it is facing.
blockRefs.tip: One step is about one dot on the screen — 10 is small, 100 is a big jump.
uses: Walk a character across the stage
Fire a bullet in the direction it faces
Step an enemy along a patrol route
Draw a line of a shape with the pen

blockRefs.what: Turns the sprite clockwise.
blockRefs.tip: 90 is a quarter turn, 180 is half, 360 is all the way round.
uses: Turn a corner when drawing shapes
Spin a fan, wheel or coin
Aim a turret step by step
Rotate a pattern in spirograph art

blockRefs.what: Pauses this script for a time.
blockRefs.tip: Use 0.1 or 0.2 for smooth animation, 1 for conversations.

explain: A sequence is instructions carried out in order, one after another. The computer never skips ahead and never guesses what you meant — it does exactly what you wrote, in the order you wrote it.
This is why the same blocks in a different order give a different result. 'Move then turn' draws a different path from 'turn then move'.
A set of ordered steps that solves a problem has a name: an **algorithm**. Children already write algorithms every day — getting dressed, making toast, walking to school.

examples.title: Order changes everything
examples.code:
move 100 steps
turn right 90 degrees
move 100 steps
examples.note: An L-shaped path. Swap the first two blocks and the shape changes completely.

examples.title: Slow it down to see the order
examples.code:
move 100 steps
wait 1 seconds
turn right 90 degrees
wait 1 seconds
move 100 steps
examples.note: Waits make an invisible sequence visible. This is a debugging technique, not just a slowdown.

deep.why: Sequence is the foundation of every program ever written. Loops, conditions and functions are all built on top of ordered steps.
deep.real: A recipe: add eggs before you bake, not after. Same ingredients, wrong order, ruined cake.
extend: Reach the same point using a different order
Write the algorithm on paper first, then code it
Act the steps out physically before coding

vocab: Sequence — instructions carried out in order, one after another.
Algorithm — a set of steps to get something done.
objectives: I can predict what a stack of blocks will do before running it.
I can put blocks in the right order to get the result I want.
I can explain why changing the order changes the result.
L1S2.hook: Give the tutor-as-robot game: the child instructs you to pick up a pen. Follow their words *exactly* and wrongly. They learn order and precision in 60 seconds.
teach: Build a 3-block script (move, turn, move) and ask the child to PREDICT the path before you run it. Prediction first, always.
Run it. Compare with their prediction. Celebrate the mismatch — that is learning.
Now swap two blocks and ask again: same blocks, different order — will it look the same? Run it.
Give them a target: 'make the sprite draw a square path'. Let them sequence it themselves.
watch: Child assumes all blocks run at once → add `wait 1 seconds` between blocks so they SEE the order.
Child expects the sprite to reset between runs → point out the sprite keeps its last position; add a `go to x y` at the start.
Blocks in a stack but the child changes the wrong number → have them read the block aloud before editing.
ask: If I swap these two blocks, will the result change? → Yes, order changes the outcome.
What is an algorithm? → A set of steps in order to do a job.
Why did the sprite end up somewhere different? → Because the steps ran in a different order.
L1S2.support: Use only two blocks and physical acting-out — walk the steps on the floor before coding them.
L1S2.stretch: Challenge: reach the same end point using a different order of blocks. Is more than one algorithm possible?

rubric.emerging: Places blocks with trial and error only.
rubric.secure: Predicts and orders a short sequence correctly.
rubric.mastered: Explains that different orders give different results and finds two algorithms for one goal.

L1S2.homework: Put 4 blocks in an order that draws a path; screenshot it.

stages.title: Set the scene
stages.goal: Get everything on the stage and reset properly, so the game starts the same way every time.
tasks: Add the backdrop (Castle 3).
Add these sprites: Gem ×3, Ghost, Dragon, Wizard.
Give each sprite a sensible size and starting position.
On every sprite add: when green flag clicked -> go to its start position, show, set size to 100%.
Test: press the green flag twice. Everything must return to exactly the same place.
stages.check: Pressing the flag twice puts every sprite back in its starting place.

stages.title: Move the player
stages.goal: Give the player smooth control.
tasks: Add: when green flag clicked -> forever.
Inside the forever, add four 'if <key pressed?>' checks — one per arrow key.
Right: change x by 4. Left: change x by -4. Up: change y by 4. Down: change y by -4.
Keep ALL FOUR ifs inside the SAME forever loop so diagonal movement works.
Test: can you move in eight directions smoothly, including diagonally?
stages.check: The player moves smoothly in all directions, including diagonals.

stages.title: Collect the items
stages.goal: Make the collectibles actually collectable.
tasks: On each collectible: when green flag clicked -> show, go to a random position.
Add a forever loop with 'if <touching Player?>'.
Inside the if: play a sound, hide, and change score by 1.
Hiding the item is what stops the score jumping up 30 times a second.
Test: collect every item. The score must go up by exactly 1 each time.
stages.check: Each item can be collected once and adds exactly one point.

stages.title: Add a hazard
stages.goal: Make it a game, not a shopping trip.
tasks: Add a hazard sprite that moves — use 'forever [move 6 steps, if on edge bounce]'.
Set its rotation style to left-right so it does not go upside-down.
On the player: if touching the hazard, lose a life and return to the start.
Add 'wait 1 seconds' after losing a life so one touch costs only one life.
Test: touch the hazard once. You should lose exactly one life.
stages.check: Touching the hazard costs exactly one life and moves you back to the start.

stages.title: Win and lose
stages.goal: Give the game clear endings, so the player always knows how they did.
tasks: Write your rules in plain English first: 'You win when ...' and 'You lose when ...'.
Add the win check: all items collected and the player reaches the goal
Add the lose check: lives reach 0
Say a message FIRST, wait 2 seconds, and only THEN use 'stop all'.
Switch to a win or lose backdrop so the ending is obvious.
Test BOTH endings deliberately — do not assume they work.
stages.check: You have triggered the win ending and the lose ending on purpose, and both work.

stages.title: Feedback and polish
stages.goal: Make every action feel good. This is what separates a finished game from a demo.
tasks: Add a sound to every important action (collect, hit, win, lose).
Add a visual effect for one action — a grow, a fade or a colour flash.
Show the score and any other variables the player needs.
Hide any variables the player does not need to see.
Test: play for 30 seconds. Can you tell what is happening without anyone explaining?
stages.check: Every action gives the player sound or visual feedback.

stages.title: Make it yours
stages.goal: Add something nobody told you to add. This is the part you will want to show people.
tasks: Add a second level with a new backdrop and more items.
Add a power-up that makes the player faster for 5 seconds.
Change the numbers until the difficulty feels right to YOU.
Ask someone else to play it and watch them silently.
stages.check: Your game has at least one feature that was your own idea.

L1S3.title: Move and turn

blockRefs.what: Moves the sprite forwards in the direction it is facing.
blockRefs.tip: One step is about one dot on the screen — 10 is small, 100 is a big jump.
uses: Walk a character across the stage
Fire a bullet in the direction it faces
Step an enemy along a patrol route
Draw a line of a shape with the pen

blockRefs.what: Turns the sprite clockwise.
blockRefs.tip: 90 is a quarter turn, 180 is half, 360 is all the way round.
uses: Turn a corner when drawing shapes
Spin a fan, wheel or coin
Aim a turret step by step
Rotate a pattern in spirograph art

blockRefs.what: Turns the sprite anticlockwise.
blockRefs.tip: Turning left 90 is the same as turning right 270.
uses: Steer a car or boat left
Undo a turn made the other way

blockRefs.what: Faces the sprite in an exact direction.
blockRefs.tip: 90 is right, -90 is left, 0 is up, 180 is down.
uses: Reset a sprite to face right at the start
Make a character face up to jump

explain: Scratch measures movement in **steps**. One step is roughly one dot on the screen, so 'move 10 steps' is a small nudge and 'move 100 steps' is a big jump. The number is a control you own — changing it changes the behaviour.
Sprites always move in the direction they are **facing**, not simply rightwards. That is why turning matters: turn first, then move, and the sprite travels somewhere new.
Turns are measured in **degrees**. 90 is a quarter turn, 180 is a half turn and 360 brings you back where you started. Every closed shape needs turns that add up to 360.

examples.title: A square path
examples.code:
repeat 4
  move 100 steps
  turn right 90 degrees
end
examples.note: 4 turns of 90 = 360, so the path closes exactly.

examples.title: A triangle path
examples.code:
repeat 3
  move 100 steps
  turn right 120 degrees
end
examples.note: 3 turns of 120 = 360. Fewer sides means a bigger turn.

examples.title: Going backwards
examples.code: move -50 steps
examples.note: A negative number moves the sprite backwards without turning it round.

deep.why: Movement plus rotation is how every character, vehicle and projectile in every game gets around.
deep.real: Turning a quarter turn to face a different wall in your room — you have been doing 90-degree turns your whole life.
extend: Work out the turn for a pentagon (360/5)
Draw a shape with the pen attached
Make the step size a variable so speed can change

vocab: Steps — how far a sprite moves (about one dot on the screen).
Degrees — how much a sprite turns. 90 is a quarter turn.
objectives: I can move a sprite a chosen distance.
I can turn a sprite by a chosen angle.
I can combine moves and turns to follow a path.
L1S3.hook: Stand up and be the sprite: 'move 10 steps' (take a step), 'turn 90 degrees' (quarter turn). Do it with your body before the screen.
teach: Demo `move 10 steps` then change 10 to 100. Ask: what changed? Establish that the NUMBER is a control the child owns.
Demo `turn 90 degrees`. Link to real turns: 90 = quarter, 180 = half, 360 = all the way round.
Build move-turn-move-turn and run it four times to trace a square. Ask them to notice the repetition (this seeds loops next session).
Set the task: get the sprite from one corner to a target using only moves and turns.
watch: Sprite drifts off-screen and disappears → drag it back, or add `go to x: 0 y: 0` at the start.
Sprite ends up upside-down → the rotation style; show 'left-right' in the sprite's Direction setting.
Child types 90 in the move block expecting a turn → read blocks aloud to separate 'move' from 'turn'.
ask: How many degrees is a quarter turn? → 90.
What happens if I change 10 steps to 100? → It moves ten times further.
How do I make the sprite go back the other way? → Turn 180, or move -10 steps.
L1S3.support: Pre-place the blocks and let the child only change the numbers, predicting each time.
L1S3.stretch: Ask for a triangle path — they must work out the turn is 120 degrees, not 90.

rubric.emerging: Moves a sprite with help; numbers changed at random.
rubric.secure: Chooses sensible step and degree values to reach a target.
rubric.mastered: Reasons about angles (square 90, triangle 120) and plans a path before coding.

L1S3.homework: Make your sprite walk a square path.

L1S4.title: Say hello

blockRefs.what: Shows a speech bubble for a set time, then clears it.
blockRefs.tip: Use this one for conversations — it tidies up after itself.
uses: Explaining the rules at the start
Announcing the score or a win

blockRefs.what: Shows a speech bubble that stays until you change it.
blockRefs.tip: It never disappears on its own — clear it with an empty say.
uses: A permanent label above a sprite
Showing a live value while debugging
A sign that stays on screen
Clearing a bubble by saying nothing

blockRefs.what: Shows a thought bubble for a set time.
blockRefs.tip: Handy for showing what a character is feeling.
uses: Showing what a character is feeling
A hint bubble in a puzzle
A character deciding what to do

explain: Speech is how sprites become characters. 'say () for () seconds' shows a bubble then clears itself; plain 'say ()' leaves the bubble on screen until you change it. That difference causes a lot of stuck bubbles.

Two sprites talking need **timing**. If both speak at once they talk over each other. Sprite B must wait roughly as long as sprite A speaks. This is a child's first experience of coordinating two independent programs.
'think' shows a thought cloud instead — useful for inner feelings, hints and comic effects.

examples.title: A timed conversation
examples.code:
when green flag clicked
say [Hi, who are you?] for 2 seconds
wait 2 seconds
say [Nice to meet you!] for 2 seconds
examples.note: The wait matches the other sprite's speaking time.

examples.title: Clearing a stuck bubble
examples.code:
say [Loading...]
wait 1 seconds
say []
examples.note: An empty say removes the bubble.

deep.why: Communicating state to the user is a core job of every interface, not just games.
deep.real: Speech bubbles in comics — you read them in order, one at a time.
extend: Time a three-sprite conversation
Use think for a character's private thoughts
Build a branching story with choices

vocab: Speech bubble — the little cloud showing what a sprite says.
Duration — how long something stays on screen.
objectives: I can make a sprite speak for a set time.
I can tell the difference between `say` and `say for seconds`.
I can sequence dialogue between two sprites.
L1S4.hook: Ask: "If your sprite could say ONE thing to the world, what would it be?" Type their exact words into the block — instant ownership.
teach: Demo `say Hello! for 2 seconds` — then plain `say Hello!`. Ask what the difference is. (Plain `say` never goes away.)
Show how to clear a stuck bubble with an empty `say`.
Add a second sprite and build a short conversation using `wait` to take turns. This is the child's first multi-sprite timing problem.
Let them write a 4-line conversation with their own words.
watch: Both sprites talk over each other → each sprite needs a `wait` matching the other's speaking time.
Speech bubble never disappears → they used `say` instead of `say for seconds`; add an empty `say` to clear.
Child writes very long text that overflows → keep bubbles under about 8 words.
ask: What is the difference between `say` and `say for 2 seconds`? → The second one clears itself.
How do I make sprite B wait its turn? → Give it a `wait` as long as sprite A's speech.
How do I clear a speech bubble? → `say` with nothing in it.
L1S4.support: Give a two-line script and let them fill in only the words.
L1S4.stretch: Ask them to time a 3-sprite conversation so nobody interrupts — real timing reasoning.

rubric.emerging: Makes one sprite speak with support.
rubric.secure: Uses say-for-seconds correctly and sequences two sprites.
rubric.mastered: Times a multi-sprite conversation so it reads naturally.

L1S4.homework: Add one more line of dialogue to your space scene.

deep.why: Communicating state to the user is a core job of every interface, not just games.
deep.real: Speech bubbles in comics — you read them in order, one at a time.

blockRefs.tip: Without a wait it's a blur — animation needs timing.

explain: A **costume** is one of the pictures a sprite can wear. Switching costumes quickly is literally all animation is — a flip-book made of code.
Costumes are also a great way to show **state**: a character that is normal, hurt or celebrating; a door open or closed; a traffic light on red, amber or green.
Timing matters as much as the pictures. Without a wait between switches, the costumes change faster than the eye can see.

examples.title: A walk cycle

forever
  next costume
  wait 0.2 seconds
end
examples.note: 0.1-0.3 seconds reads as natural movement.

examples.title: Costume as state

if <(lives) < 1> then
  switch costume to [sad]
else
  switch costume to [happy]
end
examples.note: The picture communicates the game state instantly.

deep.why: Separating what something looks like from what it does is a key idea in software design.
deep.real: A flip-book, or the frames of a cartoon.
extend: Different speeds for walking and running

L1S7.title: Your first loop

blockRefs.what: Repeats the blocks inside a set number of times.
blockRefs.tip: Blocks must go INSIDE the C-shape, not underneath.
uses: Draw a shape with equal sides
Flap wings a set number of times
Spawn a wave of exactly 10 enemies

blockRefs.what: Moves to the sprite's next picture.
blockRefs.tip: Without a wait it's a blur — animation needs timing.

blockRefs.what: Pauses this script for a time.
blockRefs.tip: Use 0.1 or 0.2 for smooth animation, 1 for conversations.

explain: A **loop** repeats the blocks inside it. Instead of dragging out 'next costume' twenty times, you say 'repeat 20' once. Less code, and changing 20 to 50 is a one-second edit.
The blocks must go **inside** the loop's C-shaped mouth. Anything placed underneath runs only after the loop has finished all its repeats.
Animation itself is a loop: swap the picture, wait a moment, swap again. Without the wait the costumes change faster than the eye can follow and it looks like a blur.
One pass through a loop is called an **iteration**. A loop inside another loop is **nested**: the inner loop runs fully on every pass of the outer one, so 3 outer x 4 inner = 12 runs.

examples.title: Walking animation
examples.code:
repeat 10
  next costume
  move 10 steps
  wait 0.2 seconds
end
examples.note: Costume change plus movement plus timing — the three ingredients of a walk cycle.

examples.title: Nested loops
examples.code:
repeat 3
  repeat 4
    move 50 steps
    turn right 90 degrees
  end
  turn right 120 degrees
end
examples.note: Draws three squares rotated around a point. The inner loop draws a square, the outer rotates it.

deep.why: Loops are how programmers avoid repeating themselves. Almost every program you use is running loops thousands of times a second.
deep.real: A chorus in a song repeats. A washing machine cycle repeats. You do not write the instructions out again each time.
extend: Change the repeat count and predict the result first
Nest a loop and work out the total iterations
Use a loop to draw a pattern with the pen

vocab: Loop — a block that repeats the code inside it.
Repeat — do something a set number of times.
Iteration — one pass through a loop.
objectives: I can use a repeat block to avoid copying code.
I can choose a sensible number of repeats.
I can explain what a loop does in my own words.
L1S7.hook: Ask the child to clap 20 times while you count. Then say: "Would you rather I wrote 'clap' 20 times, or just said 'clap 20 times'?" That is a loop.
teach: Show the long way first: four `next costume` + `wait` pairs stacked. Deliberately tedious.
Now wrap ONE pair in `repeat 4`. Run both. Same result, far less code. Let that land.
Change the repeat number and predict the effect. Establish the loop count as a control.
Task: animate the sprite walking across the stage using `repeat` with move + next costume inside.
watch: Blocks placed under the loop instead of inside it → show the C-shape 'mouth' swallowing the blocks.
Animation is a blur → a `wait` is missing inside the loop.
Child repeats the whole script instead of the repeating part → ask 'which bit actually repeats?'
ask: What does `repeat 10` do? → Runs the blocks inside it ten times.
Why use a loop instead of copying blocks? → Less code, easier to change.
Where must the blocks go? → Inside the C-shape.
L1S7.support: Pre-build the inside of the loop; the child only wraps it and sets the number.
L1S7.stretch: Ask them to nest a loop inside a loop and predict the total number of runs (a genuine stretch).

rubric.emerging: Uses a loop when told to.
rubric.secure: Chooses a loop to remove repetition and sets a sensible count.
rubric.mastered: Explains loops as repetition and uses nested loops deliberately.

L1S9.title: Forever loops

blockRefs.what: Repeats the blocks inside for ever.
blockRefs.tip: Nothing placed under a forever loop will ever run.
uses: Run an animation for the whole game

blockRefs.what: Stops the whole project.
blockRefs.tip: Say your message BEFORE stopping, or nobody can read it.
uses: End the game when you win or lose
Stop everything on a game-over screen

explain: A **forever** loop never ends. It suits behaviour that should always be on: checking for key presses, patrolling, animating, watching for collisions.
Nothing placed **under** a forever loop will ever run, because the loop never finishes. Demonstrating that deliberately saves hours of confusion later.
Several forever loops can run at the same time, on different sprites or even the same sprite. That parallelism is what makes a Scratch game feel alive.

examples.title: Constant checking
examples.code:
forever
  if <key [right arrow] pressed?> then
    change x by 4
  end
end
examples.note: The check repeats every frame, so control feels instant.

vocab: Forever — a loop that never ends until the project stops.
Condition — something that is either true or false.
objectives: I can use a forever loop for continuous behaviour.
I can explain when to use forever instead of repeat.
I can stop a forever loop.
L1S9.hook: Ask: "Which of these should run forever — a heartbeat, or blowing out birthday candles?" Sorting behaviours into 'always' and 'once' is the whole concept.
teach: Demo `repeat 10 [next costume]` then swap it for `forever`. The child sees the animation never stop.
Explain the rule: use `repeat` for a set number, `forever` for behaviour that should always be on (like checking, patrolling, animating).
Show that nothing placed UNDER a forever loop ever runs — a classic trap. Demonstrate it deliberately.
Task: make a sprite patrol back and forth forever.
watch: Blocks placed under `forever` never run → move them inside, or into a separate script.
Project cannot be stopped → use the red stop sign, or `stop all`.
Everything is in one giant forever loop → split into separate scripts, one behaviour each.
ask: When would you choose forever over repeat? → For behaviour that should always run.
What happens to blocks placed under a forever loop? → They never run.
How do you stop it? → Red stop sign or `stop all`.
L1S9.support: Give a working forever loop and have them change only what is inside it.
L1S9.stretch: Two forever loops on two sprites at once — ask them to explain how both run at the same time.

rubric.mastered: Runs several forever scripts in parallel and reasons about them.

L1S10.title: Press a key

blockRefs.what: Starts the script when a key is pressed.
blockRefs.tip: Each key needs its own script.
uses: Cheat or debug keys for testing

blockRefs.what: Starts the script when the green flag is pressed.
blockRefs.tip: Every project needs one — it's how everything begins.

explain: An **event** is something that happens which starts a script. Hat blocks are the listeners: the green flag, a key press, a click, a message.
Each key needs its **own** script. Four arrow keys means four hat blocks, each independent — they can even run at the same time.
Key events have one weakness: holding a key gives a short pause before it repeats, which makes movement stutter. That is why games usually prefer sensing (covered soon).

change x by 10

when [space] key pressed
start sound [pop]
change size by 10
examples.note: Events are perfect for one-off actions like jumping or firing.

deep.why: Event-driven programming is how nearly all modern software works — apps sit idle until you do something.

vocab: Event — something that happens and starts a script.
Hat block — the rounded block on top that listens for an event.
objectives: I can start a script with a key press.

teach: Demo `when space key pressed → say Hi!`. Press space. The magic is that the child, not the flag, caused it.
Add `when right arrow key pressed → change x by 10`. Now they are driving a sprite.
Build all four arrow keys together. Point out four separate scripts, each listening independently.
Task: drive the sprite around the stage with the arrow keys.
watch: Only one arrow works → each key needs its OWN hat block and script.
Sprite moves the wrong way → `change x by -10` for left; negative means backwards.
Nothing happens → the Scratch stage needs focus; click the stage once.
ask: What is an event? → Something that happens and starts a script.
How many scripts do I need for four arrow keys? → Four, one per key.
How do I move left? → Change x by a negative number.
L1S10.support: Set up two keys (left/right) only, and let them add up/down themselves.

explain: 'when this sprite clicked' turns any sprite into a button. This is where projects stop being animations and start being **interactive**.
Choosing the right trigger is a design decision: the flag starts the project, keys control it, clicks interact with it.

L1S14.title: X and Y coordinates

blockRefs.what: Jumps the sprite instantly to an exact spot.
blockRefs.tip: x 0, y 0 is the middle of the stage.
uses: Send a sprite home at the start of a game
Respawn the player after losing a life
Place sprites exactly when setting a scene
Reset a ball to the centre after a goal

blockRefs.what: Moves the sprite left or right by an amount.
blockRefs.tip: Negative numbers move left. This is how arrow-key movement works.
uses: Push an object when it is hit

blockRefs.what: Moves the sprite up or down by an amount.
blockRefs.tip: Negative moves down — that's how falling works.
uses: Make objects rain down the screen
Move a lift up and down

blockRefs.what: Puts the sprite at an exact left/right position.
blockRefs.tip: 'set' jumps there; 'change' moves by an amount. Very different!
uses: A paddle that follows only the mouse's x
Snap a sprite to a lane in a runner game
Reset horizontal position without changing height

blockRefs.what: Reports how far left or right the sprite is.
blockRefs.tip: Use it to check if a sprite has reached the edge.
uses: Check if a sprite reached the right edge
Score based on how far the player travelled
Decide which way an enemy should face

blockRefs.what: Reports how far up or down the sprite is.
blockRefs.tip: Used for ground checks in jumping games.
uses: Detect when a falling object is off the bottom

explain: The Scratch stage is a grid. **x** runs left to right from about -240 to 240; **y** runs bottom to top from about -180 to 180. The centre is x 0, y 0.
'go to x y' jumps instantly to an exact place. 'change x by' moves relative to where the sprite already is. Confusing **set** with **change** is one of the most common bugs at this stage.
Coordinates are how you place things precisely: resetting the player, laying out a level, or checking whether a sprite has gone past an edge.

examples.title: Reset to a known place
examples.code:
when green flag clicked
go to x: 0 y: -120
examples.note: Sprites keep their last position, so always send them home at the start.

examples.title: Set versus change
examples.code:
set x to 100
change x by 100
examples.note: The first jumps to 100; the second moves 100 further from wherever it is.

examples.title: Detecting an edge
examples.code:
if <(x position) > 230> then
  set x to -230
end
examples.note: Wraps the sprite around to the other side of the stage.

y — how far up or down (-180 to 180).

teach: Drag the sprite around and watch the x/y readout change. Let the child predict the sign before you drag (left is negative).

L1S16.title: Smooth gliding

blockRefs.what: Moves the sprite smoothly to a spot over a set time.
blockRefs.tip: Use glide when you want the movement to be SEEN, not a teleport.
uses: A fish drifting across a tank

blockRefs.what: Glides smoothly to a random spot.
blockRefs.tip: Nice for fish, bees or ghosts drifting around.
uses: A ghost floating to a new spot

blockRefs.what: Turns the sprite so it faces another sprite or the mouse.
blockRefs.tip: Put it in a forever loop to keep watching a moving target.
uses: Make an enemy chase the player
Aim a cannon at a target
Make a flower turn to follow the sun
Have a pet follow its owner

explain: 'glide' moves a sprite smoothly to a position over a chosen time, instead of teleporting. The seconds value controls how fast the journey looks.
Timing is expressive. The same journey in 0.2 seconds feels panicked; in 3 seconds it feels calm. Children discover that pacing communicates mood.
Combine glide with 'point towards' so the sprite faces where it is travelling — otherwise it slides sideways like a ghost.

examples.title: A smooth journey
examples.code:
point towards [Earth]
glide 2 secs to x: 0 y: 0
examples.note: Faces the destination, then travels there believably.

examples.title: Comparing feel
examples.code:
glide 0.2 secs to x: 200 y: 0
glide 3 secs to x: -200 y: 0
examples.note: Same distance, completely different mood.

deep.why: Smooth interpolation between two states is the basis of all animation and UI transitions.
deep.real: A lift gliding between floors rather than blinking from one to the other.
extend: A three-leg journey at different speeds
Glide to a random position repeatedly
Combine glide with costume changes

vocab: Glide — move smoothly to a place over a set time.
Smooth motion — movement the eye reads as continuous.
objectives: I can make a sprite glide instead of jump.
I can control how long a movement takes.
I can choose between glide and move for an effect.
L1S16.hook: Show the same journey twice: once with `go to` (teleport) and once with `glide` (travel). Ask which looks better in a game. They will always say glide.
teach: Demo `go to x: 200 y: 0` — a teleport. Then `glide 1 secs to x: 200 y: 0`. Same destination, different feel.
Change the seconds: 0.2 (fast) versus 3 (slow). Timing is now an expressive tool.
Combine glide with `point towards` so the sprite faces where it travels.
Task: make a rocket glide across the stage and arrive facing the right way.
watch: Glide looks jumpy → the duration is too short; try 1 second or more.
Sprite arrives sideways → add `point in direction 90` or set the rotation style.
Nothing is visible because the glide is inside a fast loop → slow it down to see it.
ask: What does the seconds number in glide control? → How long the movement takes.
When would you use glide over go to? → When the movement should be seen.
How do I make a sprite face where it is going? → `point towards` it.
L1S16.support: Pre-fill the destination coordinates so they only tune the seconds.
L1S16.stretch: Ask for a glide path with three legs at different speeds to convey a mood (panicked versus calm).

rubric.secure: Chooses glide versus go-to and tunes timing purposefully.
rubric.mastered: Uses timing expressively across a multi-leg journey.

L1S17.title: Journeys and timing

blockRefs.what: Moves the sprite smoothly to a spot over a set time.
blockRefs.tip: Use glide when you want the movement to be SEEN, not a teleport.
uses: A fish drifting across a tank

blockRefs.what: Glides smoothly to a random spot.
blockRefs.tip: Nice for fish, bees or ghosts drifting around.
uses: A ghost floating to a new spot

blockRefs.what: Turns the sprite so it faces another sprite or the mouse.
blockRefs.tip: Put it in a forever loop to keep watching a moving target.

Aim a cannon at a target
Make a flower turn to follow the sun

explain: 'glide' moves a sprite smoothly to a position over a chosen time, instead of teleporting. The seconds value controls how fast the journey looks.
Timing is expressive. The same journey in 0.2 seconds feels panicked; in 3 seconds it feels calm. Children discover that pacing communicates mood.
Combine glide with 'point towards' so the sprite faces where it is travelling — otherwise it slides sideways like a ghost.

glide 3 secs to x: -200 y: 0
examples.note: Same distance, completely different mood.

deep.why: Smooth interpolation between two states is the basis of all animation and UI transitions.
deep.real: A lift gliding between floors rather than blinking from one to the other.

L1S18.title: Backdrops and scenes

blockRefs.what: Changes the stage background.
blockRefs.tip: Backdrop code usually lives on the Stage, not a sprite.
uses: Move to a new scene in a story

blockRefs.what: Moves to the next background.
blockRefs.tip: Good for flicking through scenes in a story.

blockRefs.tip: Lets scenery drive your characters.
uses: Start enemies only when the game scene begins

explain: The **backdrop** is the picture behind everything. Changing it is how a project moves between scenes — the same trick films use.
Backdrop code usually lives on the **Stage**, not on a sprite. Sprites can react to a scene change with 'when backdrop switches to'.
Managing which sprites are visible in each scene is the real skill. Every sprite needs to know what to do when the scene changes: show, hide, or move.

show
go to x: -150 y: -50
examples.note: Scenery drives the characters — the seed of broadcasting.

deep.why: Separating scenes is how any large interactive experience is structured.
deep.real: Changing the set between acts of a play.
extend: A three-scene story

L1S19.title: Size, show and hide

blockRefs.what: Sets the sprite's size, where 100% is normal.
blockRefs.tip: Always set size at the start so it resets every game.
uses: Reset size at the start of a game
Make a boss bigger than normal enemies
Shrink a sprite that is far away

blockRefs.what: Makes the sprite bigger or smaller by an amount.
blockRefs.tip: Grow-then-shrink makes a satisfying 'pop' effect.
uses: Growing a balloon until it bursts

blockRefs.what: Makes the sprite visible.
blockRefs.tip: Put this at the start — otherwise a hidden sprite stays invisible.

blockRefs.what: Makes the sprite invisible.
blockRefs.tip: The classic bug: hiding a sprite and forgetting to show it next game.
uses: Hide an enemy that has been defeated

blockRefs.what: Makes the sprite more or less see-through.
blockRefs.tip: 100 ghost = fully invisible. Great for fading out.
uses: Fade an item out when collected
Show a sprite is invincible by flashing

blockRefs.what: Removes all visual effects.
blockRefs.tip: Add it at the start or last game's effects stay stuck on.
uses: Reset appearance at the start of a game
Remove a fade before showing again

explain: Size is a percentage: 100% is normal, 50% is half, 200% is double. **Always set size at the start**, or changes carry over between runs.
'show' and 'hide' control visibility. The classic bug is hiding a sprite at the end of a game and never showing it again, so it is invisible next time.

Graphic effects such as **ghost** (transparency) and **colour** give feedback: a fade when an item is collected, a flash when taking damage, a glow for a power-up. 'clear graphic effects' resets them.

examples.title: The reset habit
examples.code:
when green flag clicked
show
set size to 100 %
clear graphic effects
go to x: 0 y: 0
examples.note: Five blocks that prevent a whole category of bugs.

examples.title: A collect effect
examples.code:
repeat 5
  change size by 8
  change [ghost] effect by 20
end
hide
examples.note: Grow and fade together, then vanish — satisfying feedback.

deep.why: Resetting state at startup is a principle that applies to all software, not just games.
deep.real: A balloon growing then popping.
extend: Fade a title in at the start
Flash a sprite when it takes damage
Shrink distant sprites to fake depth

vocab: Effect — a visual change such as ghost (transparency) or colour.

teach: Demo `set size to 50%` and `200%`. Then `change size by 10` inside a repeat for a grow animation.

How do I make a collected item disappear? → `hide` it.

L1S19.stretch: Ask for a collect animation combining grow, fade and hide together.

L1S20.title: Adding sound

blockRefs.what: Plays a sound and carries straight on with the code.
blockRefs.tip: Use this for game effects so the action isn't paused.

blockRefs.what: Plays a sound and waits for it to finish.
blockRefs.tip: Use it when the next thing must not start too early.

explain: Sounds belong to a sprite and live in its **Sounds** tab. 'start sound' plays and carries on immediately; 'play sound until done' waits for it to finish.
That distinction is a real timing decision. Game effects should use 'start sound' so the action never pauses; a voice line that must finish should use 'until done'.
Sound is the cheapest polish available. Adding a distinct sound to every important action makes a project feel dramatically more finished.

examples.note: Each sound finishes before the next begins.

L1S22.title: Timing and waits

blockRefs.what: Pauses this script for a time.
blockRefs.tip: Use 0.1 or 0.2 for smooth animation, 1 for conversations.

blockRefs.what: Pauses until something becomes true.
blockRefs.tip: Great for 'don't start until the player is ready'.
uses: Wait for the player to press start
Hold until a sprite reaches a place
Pause until the score reaches a target

explain: 'wait' pauses **only the script it is in** — other scripts keep running. That is worth stating clearly, because children often assume it freezes everything.
Short waits (0.1-0.2 seconds) smooth animation; long waits (1-2 seconds) pace dialogue and scenes.
'wait until' is the conditional version: pause until something becomes true, such as the player pressing start.

examples.title: Pacing a scene
examples.code:

wait 0.5 seconds
say [Go!] for 1 seconds
examples.note: Waits choreograph when each thing happens.

examples.title: Waiting for the player
examples.code:
wait until <key [space] pressed?>
broadcast [start-game]
examples.note: Responds to the player instead of guessing a delay.

deep.why: Controlling timing is essential in animation, music, robotics and networking.
deep.real: The gaps in music: silence is what makes rhythm.
extend: Choreograph three sprites to a beat
Replace waits with broadcasts and compare
Use wait-until for a start gate

L1S22.hook: Clap a rhythm and have the child copy it, then clap the same claps with no gaps. Timing is the difference between music and noise.
teach: Add `wait 1 seconds` between two `say` blocks and run. The pause becomes visible.

L1S22.stretch: Ask them to sync three sprites to a beat — a genuine timing challenge.

L1S23.title: If ... then

blockRefs.what: Runs the blocks inside only when something is true.
blockRefs.tip: Usually needs a forever loop around it so it keeps checking.
uses: Jump only when on the ground
Play a sound when a key is pressed
Show a message when the score is high

blockRefs.what: Reports true when this sprite is touching another.
blockRefs.tip: Collision often fires many times a second — hide or wait to stop repeats.
uses: Detect a bullet hitting a target

blockRefs.what: Reports true while a key is held down.
blockRefs.example: forever [if <key [right arrow] pressed?> then change x by 4]
blockRefs.tip: Smoother than key events — no delay before it repeats.
uses: Run faster while shift is held
Aim while a key is down

explain: An **if** block runs the code inside it only when a condition is true. The condition slot is **pointy**, and only pointy (boolean) blocks fit — they report true or false, nothing else.

A condition is checked at the moment the if runs. That is the single biggest source of confusion: if you check once, you only find out about that instant. Games need to check constantly, which is why an if usually lives inside a **forever** loop.
You can see a boolean directly: drop 'touching Sprite1?' into a 'say' block and click it. It reports true or false. Making the invisible visible is a genuinely useful teaching move.

examples.title: Check once — usually wrong
examples.code:
when green flag clicked
if <touching [Enemy]?> then
  say [Ouch!]
end
examples.note: This tests once, the instant the flag is clicked, then never again.

examples.title: Check constantly — right
examples.code:
when green flag clicked
forever
  if <touching [Enemy]?> then
    say [Ouch!] for 1 seconds
  end
end
examples.note: Now the game keeps watching for the whole game.

examples.title: Seeing a boolean
examples.code: say <touching [Enemy]?>
examples.note: Reports 'true' or 'false' — proof that conditions are just values.

deep.why: Conditionals are how programs make decisions. Without them software could only ever do one fixed thing.
deep.real: 'If it is raining, take an umbrella.' Children already reason in conditions long before they meet code.
extend: Combine two conditions with and/or
Compare if with wait-until
Trigger different reactions for different sprites

vocab: Condition — something that is either true or false.
If — do something only when a condition is true.
Boolean — a true/false value (the pointy blocks).
objectives: I can use an if block to make code decide.
I can put a condition into the pointy slot.
I can explain why an if usually sits inside a forever loop.
L1S23.hook: Say: "IF it rains, THEN take an umbrella." Ask for three more if-then rules from their own life. They already think in conditionals.
teach: Draw the shape: `if <condition> then <action>`. Point out the condition slot is POINTY — only pointy blocks fit.
Demo `if <key space pressed?> then <say Jump!>` inside a `forever`. Crucial teaching point: without forever, it is checked once only.
Deliberately remove the forever and show it failing. The child must see WHY checking must repeat.
Task: make the sprite react when it touches another sprite.
watch: The if runs once and never again → it needs to be inside a `forever` loop.
Condition slot left empty → nothing happens; the pointy block is missing.
Child uses `if` where they need `wait until` → discuss the difference explicitly.
ask: What shape block goes in the condition slot? → A pointy (boolean) one.
Why put an if inside a forever? → So it keeps checking.
What does 'condition' mean? → Something true or false.
L1S23.support: Provide the forever loop pre-built; the child drops in the condition only.
L1S23.stretch: Two conditions with two different reactions — leading naturally into if/else.

rubric.secure: Uses if inside forever with a correct condition.
rubric.mastered: Explains conditions as true/false and chooses if versus wait-until.

L1S24.title: Sensing a touch

blockRefs.what: Reports true when this sprite is touching another.
blockRefs.tip: Collision often fires many times a second — hide or wait to stop repeats.
uses: Detect a bullet hitting a target

blockRefs.what: Reports true when the sprite touches a colour.
blockRefs.tip: Pick the colour with the eyedropper — it must match exactly.

blockRefs.what: Reports how far away another sprite or the mouse is.
blockRefs.tip: Great for 'enemy notices you when you get close'.
uses: An enemy that notices you when close
Sound that gets louder as you approach

explain: Sensing gives sprites **senses**. 'touching Sprite?' reports true whenever two sprites overlap; 'touching colour?' detects a specific colour, which is how tracks, walls and platforms are usually built.
Collision is only the trigger — you then decide what happens: score, sound, hide, bounce, lose a life. That design decision is the interesting part.

Two problems appear immediately. Collisions fire many times per second, so a single touch can score 30 points — fix it by hiding the object or adding a wait. And colour sensing needs an **exact** match, so all platforms should share one colour.

examples.title: Collecting safely
examples.code:
forever
  if <touching [Coin]?> then
    change [score] by 1
    start sound [pop]
    hide
  end
end
examples.note: Hiding the coin stops the collision repeating.

examples.title: Staying on a track
examples.code:
if <not <touching color [#444444]?>> then
  say [Off track!]
  go to x: 0 y: 0
end
examples.note: Colour sensing turns a drawn backdrop into game logic.

deep.why: Collision detection is one of the fundamental problems in game programming and robotics.
deep.real: A reversing sensor that beeps when your car gets close to something.
extend: Good and bad objects with different reactions
Colour-sensed maze walls
Use distance-to for proximity

vocab: Sensing — code that detects what is happening.
Collision — when two sprites touch.
objectives: I can detect when sprites touch.
I can react to a collision.

L1S24.hook: Ask: "In a racing game, how does the game know you crashed?" It senses the touch. Today we give sprites senses.
teach: Demo `if <touching Sprite2?> then <say Ouch!>` inside forever. Drag the sprite into the other one live — the reaction proves it.
Show `touching color` with a coloured track or wall. Use the eyedropper carefully — colour must match exactly.
Discuss what should happen ON collision: score, sound, hide, bounce. Collision is a trigger for design decisions.
Task: build a collect-or-avoid interaction.
watch: Colour sensing unreliable → the eyedropper picked a slightly different shade; re-pick from the exact pixel.
Collision fires many times per second → hide the item or add a wait so it triggers once.
Sprites look like they touch but do not → transparent edges in the costume.
ask: How does a game know two things collided? → Touching sensing.
Why might colour sensing fail? → The colour is not an exact match.
How do I stop a collision firing repeatedly? → Hide the object or wait.
L1S24.support: One collision, one reaction (a sound) — nothing more.
L1S24.stretch: Different reactions for different sprites — good and bad objects.

rubric.secure: Uses touching sensing to drive a reaction reliably.
rubric.mastered: Handles repeated-trigger problems and uses colour sensing accurately.

L1S26.title: Colour sensing

blockRefs.what: Reports true when this sprite is touching another.
blockRefs.tip: Collision often fires many times a second — hide or wait to stop repeats.
uses: Detect a bullet hitting a target

blockRefs.what: Reports true when the sprite touches a colour.
blockRefs.tip: Pick the colour with the eyedropper — it must match exactly.

blockRefs.what: Reports how far away another sprite or the mouse is.
blockRefs.tip: Great for 'enemy notices you when you get close'.
uses: An enemy that notices you when close
Sound that gets louder as you approach

explain: Sensing gives sprites **senses**. 'touching Sprite?' reports true whenever two sprites overlap; 'touching colour?' detects a specific colour, which is how tracks, walls and platforms are usually built.
Collision is only the trigger — you then decide what happens: score, sound, hide, bounce, lose a life. That design decision is the interesting part.

Two problems appear immediately. Collisions fire many times per second, so a single touch can score 30 points — fix it by hiding the object or adding a wait. And colour sensing needs an **exact** match, so all platforms should share one colour.

examples.code:
forever
  if <touching [Coin]?> then
    change [score] by 1
    start sound [pop]
    hide
  end
end
examples.note: Hiding the coin stops the collision repeating.

examples.title: Staying on a track
examples.code:
if <not <touching color [#444444]?>> then
  say [Off track!]
  go to x: 0 y: 0
end
examples.note: Colour sensing turns a drawn backdrop into game logic.

L1S27.title: Smooth controls

blockRefs.what: Reports true while a key is held down.
blockRefs.example: forever [if <key [right arrow] pressed?> then change x by 4]
blockRefs.tip: Smoother than key events — no delay before it repeats.
uses: Run faster while shift is held
Aim while a key is down

blockRefs.what: Repeats the blocks inside for ever.
blockRefs.tip: Nothing placed under a forever loop will ever run.
uses: Run an animation for the whole game

blockRefs.what: Runs the blocks inside only when something is true.
blockRefs.tip: Usually needs a forever loop around it so it keeps checking.
uses: Jump only when on the ground
Play a sound when a key is pressed
Show a message when the score is high

explain: 'key pressed?' is a **boolean** that stays true while the key is held. Checking it inside a forever loop is called **polling**.
Polling is smoother than key events because there is no key-repeat delay, and it allows **diagonal** movement: two conditions can both be true on the same pass of the loop.
All four checks must live in the **same** forever loop for diagonals to work. Separate loops fight each other.

examples.title: Smooth four-way control
examples.code:
forever
  if <key [right arrow] pressed?> then
    change x by 4
  end
  if <key [left arrow] pressed?> then
    change x by -4
  end
end
examples.note: Add up and down the same way, all inside this one loop.

examples.title: A speed state
examples.code:
if <key [shift] pressed?> then
  set [speed] to 8
else
  set [speed] to 4
end
examples.note: Nested conditions create walking and running.

deep.why: Input polling is exactly how real game engines read controllers every frame.
deep.real: Holding a button on a games controller — it keeps working while held.
extend: Convert an old project from events to sensing
Add a run key

L1S28.title: Random numbers

blockRefs.what: Gives a different random number each time.
blockRefs.example: go to x: (pick random -200 to 200) y: 150
blockRefs.tip: Keep x within -200..200 or your sprite lands off the stage.

blockRefs.what: Jumps the sprite to a random spot on the stage.
blockRefs.tip: Perfect for making targets appear unpredictably.
uses: Make a target pop up somewhere new
Place stars randomly in a night sky

explain: 'pick random a to b' gives a different whole number each time. It is what makes a game worth playing twice.
Randomness is used for **position** (where a target appears), **timing** (how long before the next enemy), **appearance** (size, colour) and **choice** (which question to ask).
Ranges must respect the stage: roughly -200 to 200 for x and -150 to 150 for y keeps a sprite fully visible. And a random value re-picked every frame makes a sprite vibrate — pick once, then use it.

L1S30.title: Keeping score

blockRefs.what: Puts an exact value into a variable.
blockRefs.tip: Always reset score, lives and timers at the start of a game.

blockRefs.what: Adds to what a variable already holds.
blockRefs.tip: Use a negative number to take away.

explain: A **variable** is a named box that stores one value you can change while the program runs. Give it a clear name — 'score', not 'thing'. Naming well is a real programming habit worth starting immediately.

There are two ways to put something in the box. **set** puts an exact value in ('set score to 0'). **change by** adds to whatever is already there ('change score by 1'). Mixing these up causes a lot of bugs.

Every variable must be **reset** at the start of the game, or the last game's score carries into the new one. Show the bug first: play, score points, run again, and watch the score continue from where it was.

Variables can be **for all sprites** (shared, like a score) or **for this sprite only** (private, so each sprite and each clone has its own copy). That distinction becomes essential once cloning starts.

examples.title: A working score
examples.code:
when green flag clicked
set [score] to 0
forever
  if <touching [Coin]?> then
    change [score] by 1
  end
end
examples.note: Reset at the start, add during play. The reset is the part beginners forget.

examples.title: Stopping a repeated score
examples.code:
if <touching [Coin]?> then
  change [score] by 1
  hide
end
examples.note: Hiding the coin stops the collision firing 30 times a second.

examples.title: A high score
examples.code:
if <(score) > (highscore)> then
  set [highscore] to (score)
end
examples.note: Only overwrite when the new score is genuinely better.

stages.goal: Get everything on the stage and reset properly, so the game starts the same way every time.

stages.title: Ask the first question
stages.goal: Build the ask-check-respond pattern once, properly.

Add 'if <(answer) = [correct answer]> then ... else ...'.
In the 'then': change score by 1 and say 'Correct!'.
In the 'else': say the right answer so the player learns something.

Add the lose check: the score is below the pass mark

L1S33.title: If ... else

blockRefs.what: Does one thing when true, a different thing when false.
blockRefs.tip: Use it when there are exactly two outcomes.
uses: Right or wrong answer in a quiz
Enough coins to buy, or not

blockRefs.what: Flips true into false and false into true.
blockRefs.tip: Reads as 'while NOT touching'.
uses: Keep moving while NOT touching a wall
Act only when the player is not hidden

explain: 'if ... else' chooses between **exactly two** paths. One of them always runs, and never both — that guarantee is what makes it better than two separate ifs.
Two ifs with opposite conditions usually work, but they can both fire if the conditions overlap, producing two messages at once. If-else cannot do that.
**Tracing** — following which branch runs and why — is one of the most valuable debugging skills a child can build.

examples.title: Win or lose
examples.code:
if <(score) > 9> then
  say [You win!] for 2 seconds
else
  say [Try again] for 2 seconds
end
examples.note: Exactly one message, every time.

examples.title: Three outcomes by nesting
examples.code:
if <(score) > 9> then
  say [Gold]
else
  if <(score) > 5> then
    say [Silver]
  else
    say [Bronze]
  end
end
examples.note: Nesting handles more than two cases.

deep.why: Branching is how programs handle the messiness of the real world.
deep.real: 'If you finish your homework you can play, otherwise you keep working.'
extend: Nest for three grade bands
Use if-else for a quiz check
Trace which branch runs and why

Trace it aloud together: 'the condition is false, so we take the else path'. Tracing is a core debugging skill.

watch: Both messages appear → two ifs used instead of if-else, or conditions overlap.
Else branch never runs → the condition is always true; test it directly.
Blocks dropped between the if and else sections → check they are in the correct mouth.
ask: When do you need else? → When there are exactly two outcomes.
If the condition is false, which part runs? → The else part.
Can both branches run? → No, only one.

L1S34.title: Repeat until

blockRefs.what: Repeats until something becomes true.
blockRefs.tip: If the condition can never be true, the loop never stops.
uses: Chase until you catch the player
Keep falling until you hit the ground
Count down until time runs out
Move until you touch a wall

blockRefs.what: Pauses until something becomes true.
blockRefs.tip: Great for 'don't start until the player is ready'.
uses: Wait for the player to press start
Hold until a sprite reaches a place
Pause until the score reaches a target

blockRefs.what: Stops just this one script.
blockRefs.tip: Useful for ending one behaviour without ending the game.
uses: End one behaviour without stopping the game
Stop a clone's loop before deleting it
End a patrol when an enemy is defeated

explain: Scratch has three loops and choosing the right one is a real skill. **repeat n** for a known number of times, **forever** for behaviour that never stops, and **repeat until** for working towards a goal.
'repeat until' checks its condition **before** each pass. If the condition is already true, the loop body never runs at all.
A loop whose condition can never become true never stops — the most common cause of an apparently frozen project.

examples.title: Chase until caught
examples.code:
repeat until <touching [Player]?>
  point towards [Player]
  move 3 steps
end
say [Caught you!]
examples.note: The chase ends exactly when it should, not after a guessed number of steps.

examples.title: Wait for a condition
examples.code:
wait until <(score) > 9>
broadcast [level-up]
examples.note: The pausing version of the same idea.

deep.why: Condition-controlled loops appear in every language as 'while' loops.
deep.real: 'Keep stirring until it is smooth' — not a fixed number of stirs.
extend: End a loop on two conditions with or
Compare all three loop types
Debug a loop that never ends

vocab: Repeat until — keep going until a condition becomes true.
Loop condition — the test that ends a loop.
objectives: I can use repeat until for goal-driven loops.
I can choose between forever, repeat and repeat until.
I can end a loop with a condition.
L1S34.hook: Say: "Keep stirring until it's smooth." Not ten times — UNTIL. Real instructions work this way.
teach: Demo `repeat until <touching goal?> [move 5 steps]`. The sprite travels exactly as far as needed, no more.
Compare all three loops explicitly: repeat (set number), forever (never ends), repeat until (goal).
Show `wait until` as the pause version of the same idea.
Task: make a sprite chase until it catches the target, then celebrate.
watch: Loop never ends → the condition can never become true; test it separately.
Loop ends immediately → the condition was already true at the start.
Child uses forever plus if when repeat-until is cleaner → compare both versions.
ask: Which loop for 'until you reach the goal'? → repeat until.
Why might a repeat-until never stop? → The condition never becomes true.
What does wait until do? → Pauses the script until the condition is true.
L1S34.support: Provide the condition; the child assembles the loop.
L1S34.stretch: Ask for a loop ending on two conditions using `or`.

rubric.emerging: Uses repeat until when given the condition.
rubric.secure: Chooses the right loop type for the job and writes the condition.
rubric.mastered: Debugs non-terminating loops and combines conditions.

L1S35.title: Follow the mouse

blockRefs.what: Makes the sprite face wherever the mouse is.
blockRefs.tip: Great for eyes that follow you, or a turret that aims.
uses: A turret that aims where you point
A magnifying glass that tracks the mouse
A shark that swims towards the pointer

blockRefs.what: Makes the sprite sit exactly on the mouse.
blockRefs.tip: The sprite will cover your pointer — offset it if that's a problem.
uses: Make a paddle or cursor sprite
Drag-and-drop feeling for a paint brush
A net that follows your hand
A spotlight that follows the mouse

blockRefs.what: Reports the mouse's left/right position.
blockRefs.tip: Use it for a paddle that slides side to side only.

blockRefs.what: Reports the mouse's up/down position.
blockRefs.tip: Combine with mouse x to follow the pointer exactly.
uses: A lift controlled by the mouse
Following the pointer in both directions

blockRefs.what: Reports how far away another sprite or the mouse is.
blockRefs.tip: Great for 'enemy notices you when you get close'.
uses: An enemy that notices you when close
Sound that gets louder as you approach

explain: Two blocks make a sprite follow the mouse: 'point towards mouse-pointer' turns it to face the pointer, and 'go to mouse-pointer' moves it onto the pointer.
Constraining the following is often better than copying it exactly. 'set x to mouse x' makes a paddle that slides horizontally but stays at its own height — the standard Pong paddle.
Following must be continuous, so it always lives inside a forever loop.

examples.title: Eyes that watch you
examples.code:
forever
  point towards [mouse-pointer]
end
examples.note: Delightful, and only two blocks.

examples.title: A Pong paddle
examples.code:
forever
  set x to (mouse x)
end
examples.note: Horizontal only — the paddle stays on its side of the court.

examples.title: Follow only when close
examples.code:
if <(distance to [mouse-pointer]) < 100> then
  point towards [mouse-pointer]
end
examples.note: Conditional following makes an enemy feel aware.

deep.why: Cursor tracking is the basis of every drawing tool and drag interaction.
deep.real: A guard dog turning its head to watch you cross the room.
extend: A paddle for a bat-and-ball game
A sprite that follows only when near
A drawing brush that follows the mouse

vocab: Mouse pointer — the arrow the player controls.
Follow — continuously move towards a target.
objectives: I can make a sprite follow the mouse.
I can make a sprite look at the mouse.
I can use following for paddles and characters.
L1S35.hook: Ask: "How does a guard dog in a game know where you are?" It points at you, constantly. Let's build eyes that follow.
teach: Demo `forever [point towards mouse-pointer]`. The sprite watches the cursor — genuinely delightful for this age.
Then `forever [go to mouse-pointer]` — the sprite becomes the cursor. Discuss when each is useful.
Show constrained following: `set x to (mouse x)` only, for a paddle that slides on one axis.
Task: build a paddle or a character whose eyes track the mouse.
watch: Sprite spins wildly → rotation style; set it to left-right or all-around as appropriate.
Sprite sits exactly on the pointer and hides it → offset with `change y by`.
Paddle moves vertically when it should not → use `set x to mouse x` only, not `go to`.
ask: How do you make a sprite face the mouse? → `point towards mouse-pointer`.
How do you make a paddle slide horizontally only? → `set x to mouse x`.
What must the following code sit inside? → A forever loop.
L1S35.support: Give the forever loop; the child chooses point-towards or go-to and tests both.
L1S35.stretch: Make the sprite follow only when the mouse is close (using `distance to`).

L1S37.title: Bouncing and edges

blockRefs.what: Turns the sprite around when it hits the edge of the stage.
blockRefs.example: forever [move 10 steps, if on edge bounce]
blockRefs.tip: Your sprite may go upside-down — fix it with rotation style left-right.
uses: A ball bouncing around the stage
Fish that turn at the tank wall

blockRefs.what: Chooses how the sprite is allowed to rotate.
blockRefs.tip: Use left-right to stop characters standing on their head.
uses: Stop a bouncing sprite going upside-down
Make a car face its driving direction

blockRefs.what: Turns the sprite by the number of degrees you choose.
blockRefs.tip: Small turns inside a loop make smooth spinning.
uses: Wobble a sprite back and forth
Rotate a shape a little between draws
Make a slow hand on a clock

explain: 'if on edge, bounce' reverses a sprite's direction when it reaches the stage edge. With 'move' inside a forever loop, that is a complete patrolling or bouncing behaviour in three blocks.
The sprite will often end up **upside-down**, because the default rotation style lets it rotate all the way round. Setting rotation style to left-right fixes it.
Starting at a random direction makes every run different, which turns one simple behaviour into an unpredictable game element.

examples.title: A bouncing ball
examples.code:
when green flag clicked
point in direction (pick random 1 to 360)
forever
  move 8 steps
  if on edge, bounce
end
examples.note: Random start direction means no two games look the same.

examples.title: An upright patrol
examples.code:
set rotation style [left-right]
forever
  move 4 steps
  if on edge, bounce
end
examples.note: The character stays the right way up.

deep.why: Reflecting off a boundary is a simple physics simulation used in countless games.
deep.real: A ball rebounding off a wall.
extend: Two bouncing sprites that react to each other
Speed that increases over time
Bounce off a drawn colour instead of the edge

L1S38.title: Patrolling enemies

blockRefs.what: Turns the sprite around when it hits the edge of the stage.
blockRefs.example: forever [move 10 steps, if on edge bounce]
blockRefs.tip: Your sprite may go upside-down — fix it with rotation style left-right.
uses: A ball bouncing around the stage
Fish that turn at the tank wall

blockRefs.what: Chooses how the sprite is allowed to rotate.
blockRefs.tip: Use left-right to stop characters standing on their head.
uses: Stop a bouncing sprite going upside-down
Make a car face its driving direction

blockRefs.what: Turns the sprite by the number of degrees you choose.
blockRefs.tip: Small turns inside a loop make smooth spinning.

Rotate a shape a little between draws
Make a slow hand on a clock

explain: 'if on edge, bounce' reverses a sprite's direction when it reaches the stage edge. With 'move' inside a forever loop, that is a complete patrolling or bouncing behaviour in three blocks.
The sprite will often end up **upside-down**, because the default rotation style lets it rotate all the way round. Setting rotation style to left-right fixes it.
Starting at a random direction makes every run different, which turns one simple behaviour into an unpredictable game element.

examples.title: A bouncing ball
examples.code:
when green flag clicked
point in direction (pick random 1 to 360)
forever
  move 8 steps
  if on edge, bounce
end
examples.note: Random start direction means no two games look the same.

examples.title: An upright patrol
examples.code:
set rotation style [left-right]
forever
  move 4 steps
  if on edge, bounce
end
examples.note: The character stays the right way up.

deep.why: Reflecting off a boundary is a simple physics simulation used in countless games.
deep.real: A ball rebounding off a wall.

teach: Demo `forever [move 10 steps, if on edge bounce]`. A patrolling sprite in two blocks.

L1S39.title: Finding bugs

blockRefs.what: Stops the whole project.
blockRefs.tip: Say your message BEFORE stopping, or nobody can read it.
uses: End the game when you win or lose
Stop everything on a game-over screen

blockRefs.what: Shows a speech bubble that stays until you change it.
blockRefs.tip: It never disappears on its own — clear it with an empty say.
uses: A permanent label above a sprite
Showing a live value while debugging
A sign that stays on screen
Clearing a bubble by saying nothing

blockRefs.what: Pauses this script for a time.
blockRefs.tip: Use 0.1 or 0.2 for smooth animation, 1 for conversations.

explain: A **bug** is a mistake that makes a program behave differently from what you intended. Debugging is finding and fixing it — and it is most of what programmers actually do.

The method matters more than luck. First state clearly what it **should** do versus what it **does**. Then narrow the search: run a single script on its own, add a 'say' to reveal a value, or add waits to slow it down enough to watch.
Change **one** thing at a time and re-test. Changing three things and finding it works tells you nothing about which one mattered.
The computer is always doing exactly what it was told. The question is never 'why is it wrong?' but 'what did I actually tell it?'

examples.title: Reveal what the code thinks
examples.code:
forever
  say (join [score is ] (score))
end
examples.note: Making an invisible value visible often solves the bug immediately.

examples.title: Slow it down to watch
examples.code:
forever
  move 10 steps
  wait 0.5 seconds
end
examples.note: If it fails too fast to see, make it slower.

deep.why: Debugging is the single most transferable skill in programming — and it teaches persistence.
deep.real: Finding out why a torch will not switch on: batteries, bulb, or switch. You test one at a time.
extend: Fix a project with two separate bugs
Keep a log of what you tried
Break a project deliberately, then swap and fix

vocab: Bug — a mistake that makes a program behave wrongly.
Debug — to find and fix a bug.
Test — to run code deliberately to see what happens.
objectives: I can describe what a program does wrongly.
I can find the block causing a bug.
I can fix a bug and re-test.
L1S39.hook: Say: "Every professional programmer's code is broken most of the day. Finding bugs is the actual job — and you're about to be good at it." This reframes failure permanently.
teach: Give the child a project you have broken on purpose. Ask first: what SHOULD it do, and what does it do instead? Naming the gap is step one.
Teach the three moves: (1) run it and watch closely, (2) click a single script to test it alone, (3) add a `say` to see what the code thinks is happening.
Slow it down with waits so the failure becomes visible.
Fix it, then re-run to confirm. Insist on the re-test — fixing without verifying is a habit worth preventing early.
watch: Child changes many things at once → change ONE thing, then test. Otherwise you cannot tell what worked.
Child deletes the whole script in frustration → encourage isolating instead; keep a copy first.
Child assumes the computer is wrong → the computer does exactly what it was told; find what it was told.
ask: What is a bug? → A mistake making the program behave wrongly.
What is the first thing to do? → Say what it should do versus what it does.
Why change one thing at a time? → So you know which change fixed it.
L1S39.support: Debug together, thinking aloud so the child hears your reasoning; then let them lead the next one.
L1S39.stretch: Give a project with two independent bugs and ask them to log what they tried.

rubric.emerging: Spots that something is wrong but not where.
rubric.secure: Isolates and fixes a bug, then re-tests.
rubric.mastered: Debugs systematically, one change at a time, and explains the cause.

L1S41.title: Winning and losing

blockRefs.what: Stops the whole project.
blockRefs.tip: Say your message BEFORE stopping, or nobody can read it.
uses: End the game when you win or lose
Stop everything on a game-over screen

blockRefs.what: Changes the stage background.
blockRefs.tip: Backdrop code usually lives on the Stage, not a sprite.
uses: Move to a new scene in a story

blockRefs.what: Sends a message that every sprite can hear.
blockRefs.tip: Name messages properly — 'game-over', never 'message1'.
uses: Start the game from a menu button
Tell every sprite the game is over
Trigger the next scene of a story
Signal that a level is complete

blockRefs.what: Runs the blocks inside only when something is true.
blockRefs.tip: Usually needs a forever loop around it so it keeps checking.
uses: Jump only when on the ground
Play a sound when a key is pressed
Show a message when the score is high

explain: A game needs rules the player can understand. A **win condition** is the test that means success; a **lose condition** means failure. Write both in plain English before writing any blocks.
Use '>' rather than '=' for score checks. If the score can jump by 2 or 5, an exact equality test can be skipped straight over and the game never ends.
Always tell the player what happened. Say the message first, give it time to be read, and only then 'stop all' — otherwise the message flashes and vanishes.
Reset every variable at the start, or a condition may already be true when the game begins and it ends instantly.

examples.title: A safe win check
examples.code:
forever
  if <(score) > 9> then
    say [You win!] for 2 seconds
    switch backdrop to [win]
    stop all
  end
end
examples.note: Message, then scene, then stop — in that order.

examples.title: A lose condition
examples.code:
if <(lives) < 1> then
  say [Game over] for 2 seconds
  stop all
end
examples.note: '< 1' is safer than '= 0' if lives could overshoot.

deep.why: Defining success and failure precisely is what turns an activity into a game.
deep.real: Any sport: you cannot play without knowing how to win.
extend: Add a draw or time-out state
Test both endings deliberately
Balance the game so it is winnable but not easy

vocab: Win condition — the rule that means the player has won.
Lose condition — the rule that ends the game in failure.
Game state — whether the game is playing, won or lost.
objectives: I can define a clear win condition.
I can define a lose condition.
I can end the game and tell the player what happened.
L1S41.hook: Ask: "How do you know when you've WON a game?" Then: "What if a game never told you?" Feedback is the point.
teach: Decide the rules together and write them in plain English FIRST: 'You win when score = 10. You lose when lives = 0.' Design before code.
Turn each sentence into an if: `if <score = 10> then [say You win!, stop all]`.
Add a backdrop change for the ending so the win feels real.
Task: give the game both endings and test each one deliberately.
watch: Game never ends → the condition is never exactly met; use `>` rather than `=` where values can skip.
Win message flashes and vanishes → `stop all` ran before the message could be read; say first, then stop.
Game ends instantly → the condition was true at the start; reset variables first.
ask: What is a win condition? → The rule that means you have won.
Why use > instead of = for a score check? → The score might skip past the exact number.
How do you tell the player? → A message and a backdrop change.
L1S41.support: Write the rules in English with them, then code only the win path.
L1S41.stretch: Add a third state — a draw or a time-out — and manage all three.

rubric.secure: Defines and codes both win and lose conditions with feedback.
rubric.mastered: Manages game states cleanly and tests each ending deliberately.

L1S43.title: Dodge and survive

blockRefs.what: Reports true when this sprite is touching another.
blockRefs.tip: Collision often fires many times a second — hide or wait to stop repeats.
uses: Detect a bullet hitting a target

blockRefs.what: Reports true when the sprite touches a colour.
blockRefs.tip: Pick the colour with the eyedropper — it must match exactly.

blockRefs.what: Reports how far away another sprite or the mouse is.
blockRefs.tip: Great for 'enemy notices you when you get close'.
uses: An enemy that notices you when close
Sound that gets louder as you approach

explain: Sensing gives sprites **senses**. 'touching Sprite?' reports true whenever two sprites overlap; 'touching colour?' detects a specific colour, which is how tracks, walls and platforms are usually built.
Collision is only the trigger — you then decide what happens: score, sound, hide, bounce, lose a life. That design decision is the interesting part.

Two problems appear immediately. Collisions fire many times per second, so a single touch can score 30 points — fix it by hiding the object or adding a wait. And colour sensing needs an **exact** match, so all platforms should share one colour.

examples.title: Collecting safely
examples.code:
forever
  if <touching [Coin]?> then
    change [score] by 1
    start sound [pop]
    hide
  end
end
examples.note: Hiding the coin stops the collision repeating.

examples.title: Staying on a track
examples.code:
if <not <touching color [#444444]?>> then
  say [Off track!]
  go to x: 0 y: 0
end
examples.note: Colour sensing turns a drawn backdrop into game logic.

deep.why: Collision detection is one of the fundamental problems in game programming and robotics.
deep.real: A reversing sensor that beeps when your car gets close to something.
extend: Good and bad objects with different reactions
