L1S44.title: Score, time and challenge

blockRefs.what: Puts an exact value into a variable.
blockRefs.tip: Always reset score, lives and timers at the start of a game.

blockRefs.what: Adds to what a variable already holds.
blockRefs.tip: Use a negative number to take away.

blockRefs.what: Shows the variable on the stage.
blockRefs.tip: Players need to see the score to care about it.
uses: Reveal a debug value while testing

blockRefs.what: Hides the variable from the stage.
blockRefs.tip: Hide working variables the player doesn't need to see.
uses: Hide working values from the player
Clean up the stage for a title screen

explain: A **variable** is a named box that stores one value you can change while the program runs. Give it a clear name — 'score', not 'thing'. Naming well is a real programming habit worth starting immediately.

There are two ways to put something in the box. **set** puts an exact value in ('set score to 0'). **change by** adds to whatever is already there ('change score by 1'). Mixing these up causes a lot of bugs.

Every variable must be **reset** at the start of the game, or the last game's score carries into the new one. Show the bug first: play, score points, run again, and watch the score continue from where it was.

Variables can be **for all sprites** (shared, like a score) or **for this sprite only** (private, so each sprite and each clone has its own copy). That distinction becomes essential once cloning starts.

examples.title: A working score
examples.code:
when green flag clicked
set [score] to 0
forever
  if <touching [Coin]?> then
    change [score] by 1
  end
end
examples.note: Reset at the start, add during play. The reset is the part beginners forget.

examples.title: Stopping a repeated score
examples.code:
if <touching [Coin]?> then
  change [score] by 1
  hide
end
examples.note: Hiding the coin stops the collision firing 30 times a second.

examples.title: A high score
examples.code:
if <(score) > (highscore)> then
  set [highscore] to (score)
end
examples.note: Only overwrite when the new score is genuinely better.

deep.why: Variables are how a program remembers. Scores, lives, health, timers, levels and settings are all variables.
deep.real: The scoreboard at a cricket match: one number that changes as the game goes on.
extend: Add a high score that survives the round

Set — put a specific value in the box.

objectives: I can make a variable and name it well.

Task: add a working score to a collecting game.
watch: Score keeps its old value between runs → missing `set score to 0` at the start.
Score jumps up by many at once → the change block is inside a fast forever loop; hide the item or add a wait.
Variable created 'for this sprite only' when it should be for all → check the option when creating it.

Hiding the item is what stops the score jumping up 30 times a second.
Test: collect every item. The score must go up by exactly 1 each time.
stages.check: Each item can be collected once and adds exactly one point.

stages.title: Add a hazard
stages.goal: Make it a game, not a shopping trip.
tasks: Add a hazard sprite that moves — use 'forever [move 6 steps, if on edge bounce]'.
Set its rotation style to left-right so it does not go upside-down.
On the player: if touching the hazard, lose a life and return to the start.
Add 'wait 1 seconds' after losing a life so one touch costs only one life.
Test: touch the hazard once. You should lose exactly one life.
stages.check: Touching the hazard costs exactly one life and moves you back to the start.

stages.title: Win and lose
stages.goal: Give the game clear endings, so the player always knows how they did.
tasks: Write your rules in plain English first: 'You win when ...' and 'You lose when ...'.
Add the win check: all items collected and the player reaches the goal
Add the lose check: lives reach 0
Say a message FIRST, wait 2 seconds, and only THEN use 'stop all'.
Switch to a win or lose backdrop so the ending is obvious.
Test BOTH endings deliberately — do not assume they work.
stages.check: You have triggered the win ending and the lose ending on purpose, and both work.

stages.title: Feedback and polish
stages.goal: Make every action feel good. This is what separates a finished game from a demo.
tasks: Add a sound to every important action (collect, hit, win, lose).
Add a visual effect for one action — a grow, a fade or a colour flash.
Show the score and any other variables the player needs.
Hide any variables the player does not need to see.
Test: play for 30 seconds. Can you tell what is happening without anyone explaining?
stages.check: Every action gives the player sound or visual feedback.

stages.title: Make it yours
stages.goal: Add something nobody told you to add. This is the part you will want to show people.
tasks: Add a second level with a new backdrop and more items.
Add a power-up that makes the player faster for 5 seconds.
Change the numbers until the difficulty feels right to YOU.
Ask someone else to play it and watch them silently.
stages.check: Your game has at least one feature that was your own idea.

L1S46.title: Capstone: plan your game

explain: A capstone is where separate skills become one project. The change is that **you** decide what to build — nobody is giving you steps to follow.
Plan on paper first: the goal, the player, the rules, and how you win and lose. Ten minutes of planning genuinely saves thirty minutes of confusion.
Build in **layers**, testing each: controls first, then the objective, then scoring, then the endings, then polish. Building everything before testing anything is how projects become unfixable.
Scope is the hardest lesson. A small finished game is worth far more than a big unfinished one.

L2S1.title: Maths in code

blockRefs.what: Adds two numbers together.
blockRefs.tip: Green blocks go INSIDE other blocks' slots.
uses: Add a bonus to the score

blockRefs.what: Takes one number away from another.
blockRefs.tip: Or use 'change lives by -1', which is shorter.
uses: Find the gap between two positions

blockRefs.what: Multiplies two numbers.
blockRefs.tip: Perfect for 'each coin is worth 10 points'.
uses: A score multiplier for a streak
Double points in a bonus round

blockRefs.what: Divides one number by another.
blockRefs.tip: Can give long decimals — wrap it in 'round'.
uses: Convert a score into a percentage

blockRefs.what: Gives the remainder after dividing.
blockRefs.tip: Brilliant for 'every 5th point, do something'.
uses: Wrap a value around a range

blockRefs.what: Rounds a number to the nearest whole number.
blockRefs.tip: Gives 4. Keeps scores looking tidy.
uses: Snap a position to a whole number
Show a clean time in seconds

explain: Green **operator** blocks calculate a value. They are not commands — they slot **inside** other blocks wherever a number is expected.
'set score to (score) + (5)' and 'change score by 5' do the same job. Understanding both matters, because the first pattern generalises to any calculation.
**mod** gives the remainder after dividing, which is how you detect 'every 5th point' or 'every other one' — surprisingly useful in games.

examples.title: Points per coin
examples.code: set [score] to ((coins) * (10))
examples.note: Nesting an operator inside a set block.

examples.title: Every fifth point
examples.code:
if <((score) mod (5)) = 0> then
  change [speed] by 1
end
examples.note: mod 5 = 0 happens at 5, 10, 15 — a clean way to escalate difficulty.

examples.title: Tidy division
examples.code: set [percent] to (round (((score) / (total)) * (100)))
examples.note: Round keeps the display clean.

deep.why: Expressions are how programs compute anything at all.
deep.real: Working out a total at the shop: price times quantity.
extend: A combo multiplier that grows with a streak
A percentage score
Speed that increases with level

vocab: Operator — a block that works out a value.
Expression — blocks combined to calculate something.
mod — the remainder after dividing.
objectives: I can use arithmetic blocks inside other blocks.
I can build an expression from a variable and a number.
I can use mod to detect multiples.
L2S1.hook: Ask: "If a game gives 10 points per coin and you have 7 coins, how does the game work out your score?" It calculates. Today code does the maths.
teach: Drop `(score) * (10)` into a `say` block. Show that green operator blocks fit INSIDE other blocks — this nesting idea is new and important.
Build `set score to (score) + (5)` and compare it with `change score by 5`. Same result, different tools; understanding both matters.
Introduce `mod`: `(score) mod (2) = 0` detects even numbers. Use it for 'every 5th point, speed up'.
Task: make a bonus that awards double points.
watch: Operator dropped beside a block instead of inside a slot → show the slot highlighting as you hover.
Division gives a long decimal → wrap it in `round`.
Child nests too deeply to read → build the expression in stages using a helper variable.
ask: Where do green operator blocks go? → Inside other blocks' slots.
What does mod do? → Gives the remainder.
How do you double a score? → Multiply it by 2.
L2S1.support: Pre-build the expression and let them change only the numbers, predicting results.
L2S1.stretch: Ask for a combo multiplier that grows with a streak.

rubric.emerging: Uses an operator block placed for them.
rubric.secure: Builds correct expressions nested inside other blocks.
rubric.mastered: Composes multi-step expressions and uses mod purposefully.

stages.title: Set the scene
stages.goal: Get everything on the stage and reset properly, so the game starts the same way every time.
tasks: Add the backdrop (Jungle).
Add these sprites: Rocks ×3, Star, Monkey.

On every sprite add: when green flag clicked -> go to its start position, show, set size to 100%.
Test: press the green flag twice. Everything must return to exactly the same place.
stages.check: Pressing the flag twice puts every sprite back in its starting place.

stages.title: Move the player
stages.goal: Give the player responsive control.

L2S2.title: Comparing values

blockRefs.what: Reports true when the first number is smaller.
blockRefs.tip: Safer than '=' because values can skip past.
uses: Game over when lives are low
Speed up when time is short
Check if a sprite is below the ground

blockRefs.what: Reports true when two values are the same.
blockRefs.tip: For letters it ignores capitals, so 'paris' still matches.

blockRefs.what: Reports true when the first number is bigger.
blockRefs.tip: Use > instead of = for scores that jump by 2 or 5.
uses: Win when the score passes a target

explain: Comparison blocks report **true or false** — they are booleans, and they fit the pointy slots in if blocks and loop conditions.
You can see this directly: drop '(score) > 5' into a say block and click it. It reports true or false. Booleans stop being mysterious once you can see one.
Prefer '>' or '<' over '=' for anything that can change by more than one. Exact equality is fragile whenever values can skip.

examples.title: Making a boolean visible
examples.code: say <(score) > (5)>
examples.note: Reports 'true' or 'false' — proof that conditions are values.

examples.title: A robust threshold
examples.code:
if <(score) > 9> then
  broadcast [level-up]
end
examples.note: Catches 10 and everything above, even if the score jumps.

deep.why: Comparison drives every decision a program makes.
deep.real: Deciding whether you are tall enough for a ride.
extend: Grade bands with several thresholds
Compare two sprites' positions
Check 'at least' correctly

vocab: Comparison — checking how two values relate.
Boolean — a value that is either true or false.
objectives: I can compare a variable with a number.
I can use comparisons as conditions.
I can choose between <, = and > correctly.
L2S2.hook: Hold up two numbers and ask 'which is bigger?' — then ask how the COMPUTER would know. It compares, and gets true or false.
teach: Put `(score) > (5)` into a `say` block and click it. It reports true or false — making the invisible boolean visible is the key move here.
Now drop the same comparison into an `if`. The child sees that conditions are just true/false values.
Discuss the classic bug: `= 10` can be missed if the score jumps by 2s. Prefer `> 9` or `>= 10`. This is real defensive thinking.
Task: trigger a level-up when the score passes a threshold.
watch: Condition using = never fires → the exact value was skipped; use > instead.
Comparison compares text not numbers → check the variable holds a number.
Child reverses < and > → read it aloud: 'score is greater than five'.
ask: What do comparison blocks give you? → True or false.
Why is > safer than = for scores? → The score might skip the exact value.
How do you check 'at least 10'? → `not (score < 10)` or `score > 9`.
L2S2.support: Give the comparison and let them test values to see true/false directly.
L2S2.stretch: Ask for a grade band system: over 90 excellent, over 70 good, otherwise keep trying.

rubric.secure: Writes correct comparisons and uses them as conditions.
rubric.mastered: Chooses robust comparisons and reasons about edge cases.

L2S3.title: and, or, not

blockRefs.what: True only when BOTH conditions are true.
blockRefs.tip: Both must be true — like 'finish dinner AND tidy up'.
uses: Win only if you reach the goal AND collect everything
Jump only if on the ground AND space is pressed
Unlock a door with the key AND enough coins

blockRefs.what: True when EITHER condition is true.
blockRefs.tip: Only one needs to be true.
uses: Accept two different answers as correct

blockRefs.what: Flips true into false and false into true.
blockRefs.tip: Reads as 'while NOT touching'.
uses: Keep moving while NOT touching a wall
Act only when the player is not hidden

explain: **and** is true only when both conditions are true. **or** is true when either is. **not** flips true and false.
A **truth table** makes this concrete: with two conditions there are exactly four combinations. Working through all four on paper is genuine computer science and children enjoy it.
When a condition becomes hard to read, store part of it in a well-named variable such as 'ready' — the same technique professionals use.

examples.title: Two requirements to win
examples.code:
if <<touching [Goal]?> and <(coins) > 4>> then
  say [Level complete!]
end
examples.note: Both must be true — reaching the goal is not enough on its own.

examples.title: Either hazard hurts
examples.code:
if <<touching [Spike]?> or <touching [Lava]?>> then
  change [lives] by -1
end
examples.note: One condition is enough to trigger damage.

examples.title: Keep going while free
examples.code:
repeat until <not <touching color [#000000]?>>
  change y by 1
end
examples.note: 'not' reads naturally as 'while NOT touching'.

deep.why: Boolean logic is the mathematical foundation computers are physically built on.
deep.real: 'You can go out if your homework is done AND it is not raining.'
extend: Draw the truth table for two conditions
Simplify a messy condition with a variable
Combine three conditions

vocab: and — true only when BOTH are true.
or — true when EITHER is true.
not — flips true to false.
objectives: I can combine two conditions with and/or.
I can use not to invert a condition.
I can predict whether a combined condition is true.
L2S3.hook: Say: "You can have ice cream IF you finish dinner AND it's not a school night." Change AND to OR and ask if that's a better deal. They will spot it instantly.
teach: Build `<touching goal?> and <key space pressed?>` and test both parts separately first, then together.
Make a truth table on paper for and/or with two conditions — four rows. This is genuine computer science and children enjoy it.
Demo `not <touching wall?>` for 'keep moving while free'.
Task: require two conditions for a win — reach the goal AND collect all items.
watch: `and` used where `or` is meant → walk the truth table; ask when it should be true.
Conditions nested wrongly so the logic inverts → build one condition at a time and test each.
Overly complex condition → split it using a variable such as `ready`.
ask: When is `A and B` true? → Only when both are true.
When is `A or B` true? → When either is true.
What does not do? → Flips true and false.
L2S3.support: Test each condition alone before combining; let the child predict the combination.
L2S3.stretch: Ask for a three-condition rule and have them draw the truth table first.

rubric.emerging: Uses a combined condition given to them.
rubric.secure: Chooses and/or/not correctly and predicts outcomes.
rubric.mastered: Reasons with truth tables and simplifies complex conditions.

L2S5.title: Timers and countdowns

blockRefs.what: Reports how many seconds since the timer was reset.
blockRefs.tip: Reset it at the start or it counts from when Scratch opened.
uses: Time how fast the player finished

blockRefs.what: Sets the timer back to zero.
blockRefs.tip: Do this when the game starts so timing is fair.

blockRefs.what: Puts an exact value into a variable.
blockRefs.tip: Always reset score, lives and timers at the start of a game.

blockRefs.what: Adds to what a variable already holds.
blockRefs.tip: Use a negative number to take away.

blockRefs.what: Pauses this script for a time.
blockRefs.tip: Use 0.1 or 0.2 for smooth animation, 1 for conversations.

explain: A countdown is a variable that decreases. The pattern is: set it to a start value, then repeatedly wait one second and change it by **-1** until it reaches zero.
The 'wait 1 seconds' is essential. Without it the loop runs dozens of times a second and the timer empties instantly.
Scratch also has a built-in 'timer' that counts **up** in seconds. 'reset timer' zeroes it — do that at the start so timing is fair.

stages.title: Set the scene
stages.goal: Get everything on the stage and reset properly, so the game starts the same way every time.
tasks: Add the backdrop (Room 1).
Add these sprites: Cat, Helper ×2.

stages.title: Make it clickable
stages.goal: Turn the target into something worth clicking.
tasks: On the target: when this sprite clicked -> change score by 1, play a sound.
Add a pop effect: repeat 3 [change size by 6] then repeat 3 [change size by -6].
After each click, jump to a random position so it must be chased.
Test: every click scores exactly one point and the target moves.
stages.check: Clicking scores a point, plays a sound and moves the target.

stages.title: Add the pressure
stages.goal: Add a timer so the game has a shape.
tasks: Create a 'time' variable and set it to 30 at the start.
Add: repeat until <(time) = 0> [wait 1 seconds, change time by -1].
The 'wait 1 seconds' is essential — without it the timer empties instantly.
When time hits 0, say the final score and stop all.
Test: the countdown takes exactly 30 real seconds.
stages.check: A 30-second countdown runs at the right speed and ends the game.

stages.title: Helpers and bonuses
stages.goal: Add depth so it is not just one button.
tasks: Add a bonus target worth 5 points that appears only sometimes.
Add a penalty target that costs 3 points if clicked.
Make the main target shrink slightly each time it is clicked, so it gets harder.
Test: all three targets behave differently and scoring is correct.
stages.check: Three different targets each affect the score in their own way.

stages.title: Win and lose
stages.goal: Give the game clear endings, so the player always knows how they did.
tasks: Write your rules in plain English first: 'You win when ...' and 'You lose when ...'.
Add the win check: the score passes your target before time runs out
Add the lose check: the timer reaches 0 first
Say a message FIRST, wait 2 seconds, and only THEN use 'stop all'.
Switch to a win or lose backdrop so the ending is obvious.
Test BOTH endings deliberately — do not assume they work.
stages.check: You have triggered the win ending and the lose ending on purpose, and both work.

stages.goal: Make every action feel good. This is what separates a finished game from a demo.

Hide any variables the player does not need to see.
Test: play for 30 seconds. Can you tell what is happening without anyone explaining?
stages.check: Every action gives the player sound or visual feedback.

L2S7.title: Lives and health

blockRefs.what: Puts an exact value into a variable.
blockRefs.tip: Always reset score, lives and timers at the start of a game.

blockRefs.what: Adds to what a variable already holds.
blockRefs.tip: Use a negative number to take away.

blockRefs.what: Runs the blocks inside only when something is true.
blockRefs.tip: Usually needs a forever loop around it so it keeps checking.
uses: Jump only when on the ground
Play a sound when a key is pressed
Show a message when the score is high

blockRefs.what: Makes the sprite invisible.
blockRefs.tip: The classic bug: hiding a sprite and forgetting to show it next game.

blockRefs.tip: Put this at the start — otherwise a hidden sprite stays invisible.

explain: Lives give the player room to fail. Three lives is a **fairness** decision: instant failure is discouraging, especially for younger children.

The classic bug is losing all three lives from one collision, because the check runs every frame while the sprites overlap. Fix it with a brief invincibility wait, or by moving the player away immediately.
**Respawning** — returning the player to a safe start position — is what makes losing a life feel survivable rather than final.

examples.title: Losing a life safely
examples.code:
if <touching [Enemy]?> then
  change [lives] by -1
  go to x: 0 y: -120
  wait 1 seconds
end
examples.note: Move away and pause, so one touch costs exactly one life.

examples.title: Game over
examples.code:
if <(lives) < 1> then
  say [Game over] for 2 seconds
  stop all
end
examples.note: '< 1' catches zero and any negative value.

deep.why: Managing state safely against repeated events is a real engineering problem, not just a game one.
deep.real: Three attempts at a penalty shootout.
extend: A health bar using costumes
A pick-up that restores health
Invincibility frames after a hit

vocab: Lives — how many attempts the player has left.
Health — a value reduced by damage.
Respawn — returning the player after losing a life.
objectives: I can track lives with a variable.
I can reduce lives on a hit and respawn the player.

L2S7.hook: Ask: "Why do games give you three lives instead of one?" Because instant failure is miserable. Fairness is a design decision.
teach: Create `lives`, `set lives to 3` at the start. Reduce with `change lives by -1` on a collision.
Solve the repeated-hit bug together: one touch drains all three lives instantly. Fix with a brief invincibility `wait 1 seconds` or by moving the player away.
Add respawn: return the player to the start position after a hit.
Task: add a 3-life system with respawn and a game-over.
watch: All lives lost from a single collision → the collision fires every frame; add a wait or move the player.
Lives carry over between games → missing reset at the start.
Game over never triggers → check for `lives < 1` rather than exactly 0.
ask: Why add a wait after losing a life? → So one touch does not drain them all.
What resets lives? → `set lives to 3` at the start.
How do you show lives to the player? → Show the variable, or use sprite icons.
L2S7.support: Provide the lives variable and the reset; the child adds the damage and game-over.
L2S7.stretch: Add a health bar using costumes or size, plus a pick-up that restores health.

blockRefs.tip: The reply goes into the 'answer' block.

blockRefs.what: Holds whatever the player last typed.
blockRefs.tip: The NEXT ask overwrites it — store it in a variable straight away.
uses: Use a typed number in a calculation

blockRefs.what: Sticks two pieces of text together.
blockRefs.tip: Remember the space at the end of 'Hello ' or words run together.
uses: Combine typed answers into a sentence

explain: 'ask () and wait' shows an input box and pauses until the player types something. Their reply lands in the **answer** block.
'answer' only holds the **most recent** reply. Ask a second question and the first answer is gone — so store anything you need later in a variable straight away.
'join' sticks text together, which is what makes a program feel personal: 'Hello Sam!' rather than 'Hello'. Remember the trailing space in 'Hello ' or the words run together.

examples.title: Remembering a name
examples.code:
ask [What is your name?] and wait
set [name] to (answer)
say (join [Hello ] (name)) for 2 seconds
examples.note: Store immediately, then reuse as often as you like.

examples.title: The overwrite trap
examples.code:
ask [Name?] and wait
ask [Age?] and wait
say (answer)
examples.note: This shows the age, not the name — the second ask overwrote it.

stages.title: Set the scene
stages.goal: Get everything on the stage and reset properly, so the game starts the same way every time.
tasks: Add the backdrop (Farm).
Add these sprites: Orange ×3, Beetle, Bowl.
Give each sprite a sensible size and starting position.
On every sprite add: when green flag clicked -> go to its start position, show, set size to 100%.
Test: press the green flag twice. Everything must return to exactly the same place.
stages.check: Pressing the flag twice puts every sprite back in its starting place.

stages.title: Move the catcher
stages.goal: Control the catcher with the mouse.
tasks: On the catcher: when green flag clicked -> forever.
Inside: 'set x to (mouse x)'. Do NOT use 'go to mouse-pointer'.
Using only x keeps the catcher at the bottom where it belongs.
Test: the catcher follows your mouse left and right but never moves up.
stages.check: The catcher slides side to side with the mouse and stays at the bottom.

stages.title: Make things fall
stages.goal: Give the falling objects their behaviour.
tasks: On a falling item: when green flag clicked -> forever.
Inside: go to x: (pick random -200 to 200) y: 180.
Then 'repeat until <(y position) < -150>' containing 'change y by -6'.
Test: items fall from random places at the top, all the way to the bottom.
stages.check: Items fall from random positions at the top down to the bottom.

stages.title: Catch and miss
stages.goal: Score catches and punish misses.
tasks: Inside the falling loop add 'if <touching Catcher?>' -> sound, change score by 1, and restart from the top.
When an item reaches the bottom without being caught, lose a life.
Add a second and third falling item with different speeds so it gets busy.
Add one BAD item that costs a life if you catch it.
Test: catching scores, missing costs a life, and the bad item punishes you.
stages.check: Catching scores a point, missing costs a life, and the bad item is dangerous.

stages.title: Win and lose
stages.goal: Give the game clear endings, so the player always knows how they did.
tasks: Write your rules in plain English first: 'You win when ...' and 'You lose when ...'.
Add the win check: the score passes your target
Add the lose check: lives reach 0 after too many misses
Say a message FIRST, wait 2 seconds, and only THEN use 'stop all'.
Switch to a win or lose backdrop so the ending is obvious.
Test BOTH endings deliberately — do not assume they work.
stages.check: You have triggered the win ending and the lose ending on purpose, and both work.

stages.title: Feedback and polish
stages.goal: Make every action feel good. This is what separates a finished game from a demo.
tasks: Add a sound to every important action (collect, hit, win, lose).
Add a visual effect for one action — a grow, a fade or a colour flash.
Show the score and any other variables the player needs.
Hide any variables the player does not need to see.
Test: play for 30 seconds. Can you tell what is happening without anyone explaining?
stages.check: Every action gives the player sound or visual feedback.

stages.title: Make it yours
stages.goal: Add something nobody told you to add. This is the part you will want to show people.
tasks: Add a golden item worth 5 points that falls faster.
Make items fall faster every 10 points.
Change the numbers until the difficulty feels right to YOU.
Ask someone else to play it and watch them silently.
stages.check: Your game has at least one feature that was your own idea.

L2S11.title: Checking answers

blockRefs.what: Asks the player a question and waits for them to type.
blockRefs.tip: The reply goes into the 'answer' block.

blockRefs.what: Holds whatever the player last typed.
blockRefs.tip: The NEXT ask overwrites it — store it in a variable straight away.
uses: Use a typed number in a calculation

blockRefs.what: Reports true when two values are the same.
blockRefs.tip: For letters it ignores capitals, so 'paris' still matches.

blockRefs.what: Does one thing when true, a different thing when false.
blockRefs.tip: Use it when there are exactly two outcomes.
uses: Right or wrong answer in a quiz
Enough coins to buy, or not

blockRefs.what: Adds to what a variable already holds.
blockRefs.tip: Use a negative number to take away.

explain: A quiz has four parts: **ask** the question, **store** the answer, **compare** it with the right one, and **respond** with feedback and a score.
The 'answer' block only ever holds the **most recent** reply. The next 'ask' overwrites it, so if you need it later, store it in a variable straight away.
Scratch's '=' ignores capital letters for words, so 'paris' matches 'Paris'. That is helpful for children's quizzes. It does not ignore extra spaces, which is a common invisible bug.
Good feedback teaches. 'Wrong' tells the child nothing; 'Not quite — the capital of France is Paris' turns a mistake into a lesson. That principle applies to your own quiz design as much as theirs.

examples.title: One question
examples.code:
ask [What is the capital of France?] and wait
if <(answer) = [Paris]> then
  change [score] by 1
  say [Correct!] for 1 seconds
else
  say (join [The answer was Paris. You said: ] (answer)) for 2 seconds
end
examples.note: One ask, one comparison, two clear outcomes.

examples.title: Grading at the end
examples.code:
if <(score) > 3> then
  say [Excellent!]
else
  say [Good try — practise and go again]
end
examples.note: Thresholds turn a raw score into meaningful feedback.

deep.why: Checking input against expected values is called **validation**, and it happens every time you log in anywhere.
deep.real: A spelling test: the teacher compares your answer with the correct one and gives feedback.
extend: Use lists so questions never repeat
Accept more than one correct spelling
Show a percentage and a grade at the end

vocab: Validation — checking whether an answer is correct.
Case sensitivity — whether capital letters matter.
Feedback — telling the user how they did.
objectives: I can check an answer against the correct one.
I can score a quiz.
I can give helpful feedback for right and wrong answers.
L2S11.hook: Ask: "If a quiz asks for 'Paris' and you type 'paris', should it be wrong?" That debate IS the lesson.
teach: Build `ask ... and wait` then `if <(answer) = Paris> then [change score by 1] else [say The answer was Paris]`.
Test deliberately with wrong capitalisation. Scratch's `=` ignores case for letters — discuss why that is helpful here.
Add the score and a final result message using a comparison.
Task: build a 5-question quiz with scoring and a final grade.
watch: Answer always marked wrong → an extra space, or comparing to the wrong variable.
Score not reset → set it to 0 at the start.
Only the last question scores → each question needs its own check.
ask: How do you check an answer? → Compare `answer` with the correct value.
Where do you add the point? → In the `then` branch.
How do you grade at the end? → Compare the score with thresholds.
L2S11.support: Provide question one fully; the child copies the pattern for question two.
L2S11.stretch: Use lists so questions are random and never repeat, with a percentage score.

blockRefs.what: Sends a message that every sprite can hear.

explain: A **broadcast** sends a message that every sprite can hear. Any sprite with a matching 'when I receive' script reacts. One signal, many reactions.

L2S16.title: Game states

blockRefs.what: Sends a message that every sprite can hear.
blockRefs.tip: Name messages properly — 'game-over', never 'message1'.
uses: Start the game from a menu button
Tell every sprite the game is over
Trigger the next scene of a story
Signal that a level is complete

blockRefs.what: Starts the script when a message is sent.
blockRefs.tip: One broadcast can start many sprites at once.
uses: Hide menu sprites when play starts

blockRefs.what: Changes the stage background.
blockRefs.tip: Backdrop code usually lives on the Stage, not a sprite.
uses: Move to a new scene in a story

blockRefs.what: Makes the sprite invisible.
blockRefs.tip: The classic bug: hiding a sprite and forgetting to show it next game.
uses: Hide an enemy that has been defeated

blockRefs.what: Makes the sprite visible.
blockRefs.tip: Put this at the start — otherwise a hidden sprite stays invisible.

explain: Real games are several small programs that hand over to each other: a **menu**, the **game**, and a **game-over** screen. Each is a **state**.
Drawing the state diagram on paper first — three boxes and arrows between them — makes the code obvious before any blocks are dragged.
Each state change is a broadcast, and **every sprite decides for itself** what to show or hide on each message. Missing one is why menu sprites float over the gameplay.
Restarting must reset everything: variables, positions, visibility. A restart that inherits the old score is the commonest bug at this level.

examples.note: Reset variables and visibility together.

examples.note: Stopping old loops prevents two states running at once.

deep.why: This is a **state machine** — a formal idea used throughout professional software.
deep.real: A board game: setup, play, then declaring a winner.
extend: Add a pause state
A settings screen

vocab: Game state — which part of the game is active (menu, playing, game over).
Scene — a distinct part of the experience.
State machine — moving between states on events.
objectives: I can build a title screen, a game and an end screen.
I can show and hide sprites per scene.
I can move between states with broadcasts.
L2S16.hook: List the screens of a game they love — menu, play, game over. "Real games are several small programs that hand over to each other."
teach: Draw the state diagram on paper: Menu → Play → Game Over → Menu. Three boxes and arrows. Children grasp this fast and it structures everything.
Each state gets a broadcast: `start-game`, `game-over`. Each sprite decides what to show or hide on each message.
Build the title screen with a start button (`when this sprite clicked → broadcast start-game`).
Task: wrap an existing game in a title screen and a game-over screen.
watch: Sprites from the menu still visible during play → each sprite needs a hide on `start-game`.
Game restarts without resetting variables → reset all variables on `start-game`.
Two states run at once → ensure the old state's loops stop, using `stop this script` or a state variable.
ask: What are the three usual game states? → Menu, playing, game over.
How do you move between them? → Broadcast messages.
What must happen when a new game starts? → Reset variables and sprite visibility.
L2S16.support: Provide the menu scene; the child wires the start button and one hide.
L2S16.stretch: Add a pause state and a settings screen — genuinely advanced state handling.

L2S18.title: Restart without bugs

blockRefs.what: Sends a message that every sprite can hear.
blockRefs.tip: Name messages properly — 'game-over', never 'message1'.
uses: Start the game from a menu button
Tell every sprite the game is over
Trigger the next scene of a story
Signal that a level is complete

blockRefs.what: Starts the script when a message is sent.
blockRefs.tip: One broadcast can start many sprites at once.
uses: Hide menu sprites when play starts

blockRefs.what: Changes the stage background.
blockRefs.tip: Backdrop code usually lives on the Stage, not a sprite.
uses: Move to a new scene in a story

blockRefs.what: Makes the sprite invisible.
blockRefs.tip: The classic bug: hiding a sprite and forgetting to show it next game.

blockRefs.what: Makes the sprite visible.
blockRefs.tip: Put this at the start — otherwise a hidden sprite stays invisible.

explain: Real games are several small programs that hand over to each other: a **menu**, the **game**, and a **game-over** screen. Each is a **state**.
Drawing the state diagram on paper first — three boxes and arrows between them — makes the code obvious before any blocks are dragged.
Each state change is a broadcast, and **every sprite decides for itself** what to show or hide on each message. Missing one is why menu sprites float over the gameplay.
Restarting must reset everything: variables, positions, visibility. A restart that inherits the old score is the commonest bug at this level.

examples.title: The state change
examples.code:
when this sprite clicked
broadcast [start-game]
hide
examples.note: The menu button hands over to the game.

examples.title: Every sprite responds
examples.code:
when I receive [start-game]
show
set [score] to 0
go to x: 0 y: -100
examples.note: Reset variables and visibility together.

examples.title: Ending cleanly
examples.code:
when I receive [game-over]
hide
stop [other scripts in sprite]
examples.note: Stopping old loops prevents two states running at once.

deep.why: This is a **state machine** — a formal idea used throughout professional software.

L2S19.title: Clones: many from one

blockRefs.key: when I start as a clone
blockRefs.what: Runs for each new clone that is made.
blockRefs.example: when I start as a clone [show, glide...]
blockRefs.tip: Each clone runs this separately with its own position.
uses: Give each falling object its own behaviour
Give each enemy its own speed

blockRefs.what: Makes a copy of a sprite while the game runs.
blockRefs.tip: One sprite plus clones beats making 50 sprites by hand.

blockRefs.what: Removes this clone.
blockRefs.tip: Always delete clones when done or the project slows to a crawl.
uses: Remove a bullet that left the screen
Clear enemies at the end of a wave

explain: A **clone** is a copy of a sprite created while the project is running. One asteroid sprite plus clones can become fifty asteroids on screen — without you making fifty sprites by hand.

Cloning has three parts and all three matter. A **spawner** creates clones. A **'when I start as a clone'** script says what each clone does — it runs separately for every clone. And **'delete this clone'** cleans up, because clones that are never deleted pile up and grind the project to a halt.
Each clone can behave differently if you give it its own values. A variable made **for this sprite only** gives every clone a private copy, so one can be fast and another slow.
Clones inherit the original's position, size and costume at the moment they are created — so set those before cloning if you want variety.

examples.title: The spawner
examples.code:
when green flag clicked
hide
forever
  create clone of [myself]
  wait 1 seconds
end
examples.note: The original hides; only the clones are seen.

examples.title: What each clone does
examples.code:
when I start as a clone
go to x: (pick random -200 to 200) y: 180
show
repeat until <(y position) < -170>
  change y by -5
end
delete this clone
examples.note: Random x gives every clone a different path. The delete keeps performance healthy.

examples.title: Clones with their own speed
examples.code:
when I start as a clone
set [speed] to (pick random 3 to 8)
forever
  change y by (0 - (speed))
end
examples.note: 'speed' must be a for-this-sprite-only variable or every clone shares one value.

deep.why: Cloning is the first taste of creating objects at runtime — the same idea behind every enemy, bullet and particle in real games.
deep.real: One cookie cutter making hundreds of biscuits: one shape, many copies, each going its own way.
extend: Two clone types — one good, one harmful
Waves that get faster each round
Formations built by calculating positions

explain: Waves are a design tool. 'repeat 10 [create clone, wait 0.2]' produces a burst of ten enemies rather than an endless stream, which lets you pace difficulty.
Giving each clone its own **for this sprite only** variable is what makes cloning powerful: one sprite can produce fast enemies, slow enemies, and bonus items.
Formations come from **calculating** positions in a loop rather than randomising them — that is how synchronised patterns and enemy grids are built.
Performance is a genuine constraint. Cap the number of clones and delete them when they leave the screen.

  wait 0.2 seconds

Add the lose check: you run out of lives or time

L2S24.title: Lists: storing many values

blockRefs.what: Adds an item to the end of a list.
blockRefs.tip: Lists hold many values; a variable holds only one.

blockRefs.tip: This pattern picks a random item safely.

blockRefs.tip: Handy for checking an answer against many possibilities.

explain: A variable holds **one** value. A **list** holds many, numbered from 1. In Scratch the first item is item 1, not item 0 — worth saying out loud, because most programming languages start at 0 and this trips people up later.
Lists unlock whole categories of project: quizzes with many questions, high-score tables, word games, inventories, and anything that stores a history.

The most useful pattern is picking a random item safely: 'item (pick random 1 to (length of list)) of list'. Using the length rather than a fixed number means the code still works when you add more items.
**Parallel lists** are two lists kept in step, so item 3 of 'questions' matches item 3 of 'answers'. Keeping them aligned is the programmer's responsibility — nothing enforces it for you.

examples.title: Filling a list once
examples.code:
when green flag clicked
delete all of [questions]
add [What is 2+2?] to [questions]
add [What is 5x3?] to [questions]
examples.note: Clear before adding, or the list doubles in length every run.

examples.title: Picking a random item
examples.code:
set [n] to (pick random 1 to (length of [questions]))
ask (item (n) of [questions]) and wait
examples.note: Using length means the code adapts as the list grows.

examples.title: Parallel lists
examples.code:
if <(answer) = (item (n) of [answers])> then
  change [score] by 1
end
examples.note: Question n and answer n line up, so one index checks both.

deep.why: Lists are the first data structure. Databases, spreadsheets and search engines are all built on the idea of ordered, indexed data.
deep.real: A shopping list, a register, a playlist — all numbered collections you already use.
extend: Store a top-three high score table
Remove questions as they are used so none repeat
Use 'contains' to accept several correct spellings

watch: Off-by-one confusion → Scratch lists start at 1, not 0; say it explicitly.
Items duplicate every run → `delete all of list` before adding, or add items only once.

explain: A variable holds **one** value. A **list** holds many, numbered from 1. In Scratch the first item is item 1, not item 0 — worth saying out loud, because most programming languages start at 0 and this trips people up later.
Lists unlock whole categories of project: quizzes with many questions, high-score tables, word games, inventories, and anything that stores a history.

The most useful pattern is picking a random item safely: 'item (pick random 1 to (length of list)) of list'. Using the length rather than a fixed number means the code still works when you add more items.
**Parallel lists** are two lists kept in step, so item 3 of 'questions' matches item 3 of 'answers'. Keeping them aligned is the programmer's responsibility — nothing enforces it for you.

examples.title: Filling a list once
examples.code:
when green flag clicked
delete all of [questions]
add [What is 2+2?] to [questions]
add [What is 5x3?] to [questions]
examples.note: Clear before adding, or the list doubles in length every run.

examples.title: Picking a random item
examples.code:
set [n] to (pick random 1 to (length of [questions]))
ask (item (n) of [questions]) and wait
examples.note: Using length means the code adapts as the list grows.

examples.title: Parallel lists
examples.code:
if <(answer) = (item (n) of [answers])> then
  change [score] by 1
end
examples.note: Question n and answer n line up, so one index checks both.

L2S27.title: Make your own blocks

blockRefs.what: The script that says what your own block does.
blockRefs.tip: Name it in plain English — 'reset player', not 'block1'.

blockRefs.what: A block you invented, used like any other block.
blockRefs.tip: Move repeated code here and your main script gets much clearer.
uses: Call your reset routine at the start
Keep the main script short and readable

explain: A **custom block** is a block you invent. You give it a name, define what it does, and then use it exactly like any built-in block.
The motivation is real duplication. When the same six blocks appear in three places, that is three places to fix when something changes. Move them into 'reset player' and there is one.
This is **abstraction** — hiding detail behind a meaningful name. 'Make a cup of tea' is one instruction that hides twelve steps. Good code reads like a list of intentions, not a wall of blocks.
Adding an **input** makes one block serve many cases. 'draw square (size)' replaces separate blocks for every size you might want.

examples.title: Before: repeated everywhere
examples.code:

set [lives] to 3
set [score] to 0
show
set size to 100 %
examples.note: Now imagine this same stack copied into three different scripts.

examples.title: After: one named block
examples.code:
define [reset player]
go to x: 0 y: -100
set [lives] to 3
set [score] to 0
show
set size to 100 %
examples.note: The main script becomes simply 'reset player'.

examples.title: With an input
examples.code:
define [draw square (size)]
repeat 4
  move (size) steps
  turn right 90 degrees
end
examples.note: 'draw square (50)' and 'draw square (200)' now both work from one definition.

L2S29.title: Blocks with inputs

blockRefs.what: Your own block that takes a value.
blockRefs.tip: Drag the orange input from the hat into the blocks inside.

blockRefs.what: Uses your block with a value you choose.
blockRefs.tip: One block with an input beats five nearly identical blocks.

explain: An **input** (parameter) lets one custom block handle many situations. Instead of 'jump small' and 'jump big', you build 'jump (height)'.
The step children miss is **dragging the orange parameter** from the define hat into the blocks inside. Without that the block ignores its input and always uses a fixed number.
Name inputs meaningfully — 'size' and 'amount', not 'a' and 'b'. The name is what makes the block readable when you use it later.

examples.title: A parameterised block
examples.code:

repeat 4
  move (size) steps
  turn right 90 degrees
end
examples.note: The orange 'size' must be dragged into the move block.

examples.code:

draw square (100)
draw square (150)
examples.note: One definition, three different results.

examples.title: Two inputs
examples.code: define [damage (amount) to (target)]
examples.note: Multiple parameters make a block genuinely reusable.

deep.why: This is exactly how functions with arguments work in every programming language.
deep.real: A recipe that says 'serves N' — the same method scaled to a number you choose.

L2S31.title: Gravity and jumping

blockRefs.what: Moves the sprite up or down by an amount.
blockRefs.tip: Negative moves down — that's how falling works.
uses: Make objects rain down the screen
Move a lift up and down

blockRefs.what: Puts an exact value into a variable.
blockRefs.tip: Always reset score, lives and timers at the start of a game.

blockRefs.what: Adds to what a variable already holds.
blockRefs.tip: Use a negative number to take away.

blockRefs.what: Runs the blocks inside only when something is true.
blockRefs.tip: Usually needs a forever loop around it so it keeps checking.
uses: Jump only when on the ground
Play a sound when a key is pressed
Show a message when the score is high

explain: Real gravity does not move things at a constant speed — it makes them **speed up** as they fall. To model that you need two variables working together: **position** and **velocity**.

The pattern is short but powerful. Every frame, velocity changes the position ('change y by velocity'), and gravity changes the velocity ('change velocity by -1'). Because velocity keeps growing more negative, the fall accelerates — exactly like a dropped pen.

Jumping is simply setting velocity to a positive number **once**. Gravity then takes over automatically and produces a natural arc. If a child sets velocity every frame, the sprite floats instead of arcing.
You always need a **ground check**, or the sprite falls forever. When it reaches the floor, snap it to floor level and set velocity back to 0.

examples.title: Gravity
examples.code:
when green flag clicked
set [velocity] to 0
forever
  change y by (velocity)
  change [velocity] by -1
end
examples.note: Two lines produce real accelerating motion.

examples.title: Jumping
examples.code:
when [space] key pressed
if <(y position) < -119> then
  set [velocity] to 12
end
examples.note: Set velocity once, and only when standing on the ground — that also prevents mid-air jumping.

examples.title: The ground check
examples.code:
if <(y position) < -120> then
  set y to -120
  set [velocity] to 0
end
examples.note: Stops the fall and resets velocity so the next jump works.

deep.why: This is a real physics simulation — the same velocity-and-acceleration model used in professional game engines.
deep.real: Drop a pen and watch: it starts slow and speeds up. It does not fall at one constant speed.
extend: Tune gravity and jump height for different feels
Add a double jump with a counter
Make jump height depend on how long space is held

vocab: Velocity — speed and direction of movement.
Gravity — a constant downward pull.
Physics — modelling real movement with numbers.
objectives: I can model gravity with a velocity variable.
I can make a sprite jump and fall naturally.
I can tune values to change the feel.
L2S31.hook: Drop a pen and ask: "Did it fall at the same speed the whole way?" No — it sped up. Real gravity accelerates, and so will their code.
teach: Explain the two-variable pattern in plain words: velocity changes the position, gravity changes the velocity.
Build it: `forever [change y by (velocity), change velocity by -1]`. Watch the sprite accelerate downward — that curve is real physics.
Add jump: `set velocity to 12` on space. Add the ground check: `if <y position < -120> then [set y to -120, set velocity to 0]`.
Tune together: gravity -1 versus -0.5, jump 12 versus 20. Feel is a design decision.
watch: Sprite falls through the floor → the ground check is missing or the boundary is wrong.
Jump is instant with no arc → velocity is being set every frame; set it once on the key press.
Infinite jumping in mid-air → only allow a jump when on the ground.
ask: What does the velocity variable do? → Controls how fast and which way the sprite moves vertically.
What does gravity do to velocity? → Reduces it every frame.
How do you stop mid-air jumping? → Check the sprite is on the ground first.

L2S31.stretch: Add double-jump, or variable jump height based on how long space is held.

L2S33.title: Platform collision

blockRefs.what: Reports true when the sprite touches a colour.
blockRefs.tip: Pick the colour with the eyedropper — it must match exactly.

blockRefs.what: Moves the sprite up or down by an amount.
blockRefs.tip: Negative moves down — that's how falling works.
uses: Make objects rain down the screen
Move a lift up and down

blockRefs.what: Moves the sprite left or right by an amount.
blockRefs.tip: Negative numbers move left. This is how arrow-key movement works.
uses: Push an object when it is hit

blockRefs.what: Repeats until something becomes true.
blockRefs.tip: If the condition can never be true, the loop never stops.
uses: Chase until you catch the player
Keep falling until you hit the ground
Count down until time runs out
Move until you touch a wall

explain: A platform game needs the player to **stand on** solid ground. The usual approach is colour sensing: make every platform exactly the same colour and check for it.

Detection is only half the job. **Collision resolution** is what happens next: if the player has sunk into a platform, move them up one step at a time until they are free. Teleporting them looks wrong; stepping out looks right.
Handle horizontal and vertical collision **separately**, or the player sticks to walls. This is the same approach real 2D engines use.

examples.title: Standing on ground
examples.code:
repeat until <not <touching color [#7f7f7f]?>>
  change y by 1
end
set [velocity] to 0
examples.note: Climb out of the platform one pixel at a time.

examples.title: Blocking a wall
examples.code:
change x by 4
if <touching color [#7f7f7f]?> then
  change x by -4
end
examples.note: Move, test, and undo the move if it was invalid.

deep.why: Separating detection from resolution is exactly how professional physics engines are structured.
deep.real: You cannot walk through a wall — something has to push you back.
extend: Moving platforms
One-way platforms you can jump up through
A level with three platforms and a goal

vocab: Platform — a surface the player can stand on.
Collision resolution — pushing the player out of a wall.
Hitbox — the area used for collision.
objectives: I can detect standing on a platform.
I can stop the player passing through walls.

L2S33.hook: Ask: "In Mario, what stops you falling through the floor?" The game checks, every frame, and pushes you back up.
teach: Use one colour for all solid ground. Consistency makes collision reliable — a real design constraint.
Teach the push-out pattern: `repeat until <not <touching color?>> [change y by 1]` — climb out of the ground rather than teleporting.
Handle horizontal collision the same way so the player cannot walk through walls.
Task: build a level with three platforms the player can traverse.
watch: Player sinks into the ground → the push-out loop is missing.
Player sticks to walls → separate the x and y collision checks.
Collision unreliable → platform colours are slightly different shades; use one exact colour.
ask: How does the game know you are standing on something? → Colour or sprite sensing below the player.
What do you do when stuck inside a platform? → Move out one step at a time until free.
Why use a single platform colour? → So one check works everywhere.

L2S33.stretch: Add moving platforms or one-way platforms.

L2S34.title: Build a level

blockRefs.what: Reports true when the sprite touches a colour.
blockRefs.tip: Pick the colour with the eyedropper — it must match exactly.

blockRefs.what: Moves the sprite up or down by an amount.
blockRefs.tip: Negative moves down — that's how falling works.
uses: Make objects rain down the screen
Move a lift up and down

blockRefs.what: Moves the sprite left or right by an amount.
blockRefs.tip: Negative numbers move left. This is how arrow-key movement works.
uses: Push an object when it is hit

blockRefs.what: Repeats until something becomes true.
blockRefs.tip: If the condition can never be true, the loop never stops.
uses: Chase until you catch the player
Keep falling until you hit the ground
Count down until time runs out
Move until you touch a wall

explain: A platform game needs the player to **stand on** solid ground. The usual approach is colour sensing: make every platform exactly the same colour and check for it.

Detection is only half the job. **Collision resolution** is what happens next: if the player has sunk into a platform, move them up one step at a time until they are free. Teleporting them looks wrong; stepping out looks right.
Handle horizontal and vertical collision **separately**, or the player sticks to walls. This is the same approach real 2D engines use.

examples.title: Standing on ground
examples.code:
repeat until <not <touching color [#7f7f7f]?>>
  change y by 1
end
set [velocity] to 0
examples.note: Climb out of the platform one pixel at a time.

examples.title: Blocking a wall
examples.code:
change x by 4
if <touching color [#7f7f7f]?> then
  change x by -4
end
examples.note: Move, test, and undo the move if it was invalid.

deep.why: Separating detection from resolution is exactly how professional physics engines are structured.
deep.real: You cannot walk through a wall — something has to push you back.

L2S35.title: Drawing with the pen

blockRefs.what: Starts drawing a line as the sprite moves.
blockRefs.tip: Needs the Pen extension, added from the bottom-left button.
uses: Draw a trail behind a sprite

blockRefs.what: Stops drawing.
blockRefs.tip: Lift the pen before moving into position, or you draw a stray line.
uses: Reposition before starting a new line

blockRefs.what: Clears everything drawn on the stage.
blockRefs.tip: Start every pen project with this or old drawings pile up.
uses: Clear the canvas at the start

blockRefs.what: Chooses the colour to draw with.
blockRefs.tip: Change it inside a loop for rainbow patterns.
uses: Match the pen to a theme

blockRefs.what: Chooses how thick the line is.
blockRefs.tip: Thick lines for bold art, thin for detail.

explain: The **pen** turns a sprite into a paintbrush: while the pen is down, the sprite leaves a line wherever it moves.

Pen blocks are an **extension** — they are not in the palette until you add them from the button at the bottom left. Children need to know extensions exist, because Music, Video Sensing and Text to Speech all work the same way.
Every pen project should start with 'erase all' and 'pen up'. Without them, drawings from the previous run stay on the stage and stray lines appear as the sprite moves into position.
Pen plus loops is where maths becomes visible. Any regular shape needs turns totalling 360, so the turn is always 360 divided by the number of sides.

examples.title: A clean start
examples.code:
when green flag clicked
erase all
pen up
go to x: 0 y: 0
pen down
examples.note: Clear, lift, position, then start drawing. This order prevents stray lines.

examples.title: Any regular polygon
examples.code:
set [sides] to 6
repeat (sides)
  move 60 steps
  turn right ((360) / (sides)) degrees
end
examples.note: Change 'sides' to 3, 5 or 8 and the same code draws a triangle, pentagon or octagon.

examples.title: A rainbow spiral
examples.code:
repeat 36
  repeat 4
    move 100 steps
    turn right 90 degrees
  end
  turn right 10 degrees
  change pen color by 5
end
examples.note: 36 x 10 = 360, so the pattern closes perfectly into a circle.

deep.why: Drawing with code is how data visualisation, computer graphics and CAD software all begin.
deep.real: A spirograph toy, or drawing round and round on paper without lifting your pencil.

Draw a graph of a variable

L2S37.title: Geometric art

blockRefs.what: Repeats the blocks inside a set number of times.
blockRefs.tip: Blocks must go INSIDE the C-shape, not underneath.
uses: Draw a shape with equal sides
Flap wings a set number of times
Spawn a wave of exactly 10 enemies

blockRefs.what: Turns the sprite by the number of degrees you choose.
blockRefs.tip: Small turns inside a loop make smooth spinning.
uses: Wobble a sprite back and forth
Rotate a shape a little between draws
Make a slow hand on a clock

blockRefs.what: Shifts the pen colour a little.
blockRefs.tip: This is how rainbow spirographs are made.
uses: Colour that shifts as a sprite moves

blockRefs.what: Chooses how thick the line is.
blockRefs.tip: Thick lines for bold art, thin for detail.

blockRefs.what: Gives a different random number each time.
blockRefs.example: go to x: (pick random -200 to 200) y: 150
blockRefs.tip: Keep x within -200..200 or your sprite lands off the stage.

explain: Nested loops plus rotation produce spirograph art. The inner loop draws one shape; the outer loop rotates and repeats it.
The maths must agree: repeats multiplied by the turn angle should total 360, or the pattern will not close into a circle. 36 x 10 = 360; 18 x 20 = 360.

Changing the pen colour in the **outer** loop gives a rainbow across the whole pattern. Putting it in the inner loop changes colour within each shape instead — both are valid, and comparing them is a good experiment.

examples.title: A classic spirograph
examples.code:
repeat 36
  repeat 4
    move 100 steps
    turn right 90 degrees
  end
  turn right 10 degrees
  change pen color by 5
end
examples.note: Square, rotate 10 degrees, repeat 36 times — a full circle of squares.

examples.title: Any shape, any rotation
examples.code:
set [sides] to 6
repeat 24
  repeat (sides)
    move 60 steps
    turn right ((360) / (sides)) degrees
  end
  turn right 15 degrees
end
examples.note: 24 x 15 = 360, and the shape is controlled by one variable.

deep.why: Generative art is a real creative field, and it is pure loops and maths.
deep.real: A spirograph toy, or the patterns in a kaleidoscope.
extend: Design a pattern to a specification
Make it denser or sparser and explain why

vocab: Nested loop — a loop inside another loop.
Pattern — a repeating design.
Spirograph — art from repeated rotated shapes.
objectives: I can nest loops to create patterns.

L2S37.hook: Show a spirograph image. "Twelve lines of code made that. Let's find out how."
teach: Build the nested loop: `repeat 36 [ repeat 4 [move 100, turn 90], turn 10 ]`. Square, rotate, repeat.
Do the maths together: 36 x 10 = 360, a full circle. Children love that the numbers must agree.
Add `change pen color by 5` inside the outer loop for a rainbow effect.
Task: invent a pattern by changing the shape, the rotation and the repeat count.
watch: Pattern does not close into a circle → repeats multiplied by the turn must equal 360.
Drawing runs off-stage → reduce the move distance.
Colour never changes → the change-pen-colour block is in the wrong loop.
ask: Why 36 repeats and 10 degrees? → Together they make 360, a full circle.
What does the inner loop draw? → One shape.
How do you get a rainbow? → Change pen colour each time round the outer loop.

L2S38.title: Spirograph patterns

blockRefs.what: Repeats the blocks inside a set number of times.
blockRefs.tip: Blocks must go INSIDE the C-shape, not underneath.
uses: Draw a shape with equal sides
Flap wings a set number of times
Spawn a wave of exactly 10 enemies

blockRefs.what: Turns the sprite by the number of degrees you choose.
blockRefs.tip: Small turns inside a loop make smooth spinning.
uses: Wobble a sprite back and forth
Rotate a shape a little between draws
Make a slow hand on a clock

blockRefs.what: Shifts the pen colour a little.
blockRefs.tip: This is how rainbow spirographs are made.
uses: Colour that shifts as a sprite moves

blockRefs.what: Chooses how thick the line is.
blockRefs.tip: Thick lines for bold art, thin for detail.

blockRefs.what: Gives a different random number each time.
blockRefs.example: go to x: (pick random -200 to 200) y: 150
blockRefs.tip: Keep x within -200..200 or your sprite lands off the stage.

explain: Nested loops plus rotation produce spirograph art. The inner loop draws one shape; the outer loop rotates and repeats it.
The maths must agree: repeats multiplied by the turn angle should total 360, or the pattern will not close into a circle. 36 x 10 = 360; 18 x 20 = 360.

Changing the pen colour in the **outer** loop gives a rainbow across the whole pattern. Putting it in the inner loop changes colour within each shape instead — both are valid, and comparing them is a good experiment.

examples.title: A classic spirograph
examples.code:
repeat 36
  repeat 4
    move 100 steps
    turn right 90 degrees
  end
  turn right 10 degrees
  change pen color by 5
end
examples.note: Square, rotate 10 degrees, repeat 36 times — a full circle of squares.

examples.title: Any shape, any rotation
examples.code:
set [sides] to 6
repeat 24
  repeat (sides)
    move 60 steps
    turn right ((360) / (sides)) degrees
  end
  turn right 15 degrees
end
examples.note: 24 x 15 = 360, and the shape is controlled by one variable.

deep.why: Generative art is a real creative field, and it is pure loops and maths.
deep.real: A spirograph toy, or the patterns in a kaleidoscope.
extend: Design a pattern to a specification
Make it denser or sparser and explain why
Randomise colours and sizes

vocab: Nested loop — a loop inside another loop.
Pattern — a repeating design.
Spirograph — art from repeated rotated shapes.
objectives: I can nest loops to create patterns.
I can vary colour across a drawing.
I can predict a pattern from its code.
L2S38.hook: Show a spirograph image. "Twelve lines of code made that. Let's find out how."
teach: Build the nested loop: `repeat 36 [ repeat 4 [move 100, turn 90], turn 10 ]`. Square, rotate, repeat.
Do the maths together: 36 x 10 = 360, a full circle. Children love that the numbers must agree.
Add `change pen color by 5` inside the outer loop for a rainbow effect.
Task: invent a pattern by changing the shape, the rotation and the repeat count.
watch: Pattern does not close into a circle → repeats multiplied by the turn must equal 360.
Drawing runs off-stage → reduce the move distance.
Colour never changes → the change-pen-colour block is in the wrong loop.
ask: Why 36 repeats and 10 degrees? → Together they make 360, a full circle.
What does the inner loop draw? → One shape.
How do you get a rainbow? → Change pen colour each time round the outer loop.

L2S39.title: Music with code

blockRefs.what: Plays a drum sound for a number of beats.
blockRefs.tip: Needs the Music extension. Put it in a loop to make a rhythm.

blockRefs.what: Plays a musical note for a number of beats.
blockRefs.tip: 60 is middle C. Higher numbers are higher notes.

blockRefs.what: Sets how fast the music plays.
blockRefs.tip: Bigger number = faster music.
uses: Speed a song up as the level gets harder
Slow music for a calm scene
Match two parts to the same speed

blockRefs.what: A silent gap in the music.
blockRefs.tip: Silence is part of rhythm — it's what makes a beat groove.
uses: Gaps that make a rhythm groove

explain: The Music extension adds drums and notes. A **beat** is the unit of musical time; **tempo** controls how fast beats go; notes are numbered, with 60 as middle C.
Rhythm is repetition, so loops are the natural tool. A one-bar drum pattern in a repeat loop becomes a groove.
Two parts must start together or they drift. Trigger both with the **same broadcast** rather than two separate flag clicks — a genuine reason to use messages.
Silence matters: 'rest' is what gives a rhythm its shape.

examples.title: A drum loop
examples.code:
set tempo to 100
forever
  play drum (1) for 0.25 beats
  rest for 0.25 beats
  play drum (2) for 0.25 beats
  rest for 0.25 beats
end
examples.note: Rests are as important as the hits.

examples.title: A melody
examples.code:
play note (60) for 0.5 beats
play note (62) for 0.5 beats
play note (64) for 1 beats
examples.note: 60, 62, 64 walks up the scale.

examples.title: Two parts in sync
examples.code:
when I receive [play-music]
forever
  play drum (1) for 0.5 beats
end
examples.note: Both sprites receive the same message, so they start together.

deep.why: Music software is built on exactly these ideas: timing, loops and synchronisation.
deep.real: Clapping a rhythm together — everyone has to start on the same beat.
extend: A three-layer piece
Tempo that speeds up with difficulty
A clickable piano

stages.title: Set the scene
stages.goal: Get everything on the stage and reset properly, so the game starts the same way every time.
tasks: Add the backdrop (Chalkboard).
Add these sprites: Gobo.
Give each sprite a sensible size and starting position.
On every sprite add: when green flag clicked -> go to its start position, show, set size to 100%.
Test: press the green flag twice. Everything must return to exactly the same place.
stages.check: Pressing the flag twice puts every sprite back in its starting place.

stages.title: Ask the first question
stages.goal: Build the ask-check-respond pattern once, properly.
tasks: Add 'ask [your question] and wait'.
Add 'if <(answer) = [correct answer]> then ... else ...'.
In the 'then': change score by 1 and say 'Correct!'.
In the 'else': say the right answer so the player learns something.
Test: try a right answer AND a wrong answer.
stages.check: One question scores correctly and gives useful feedback either way.

stages.title: Build the full quiz
stages.goal: Turn one question into a real quiz.
tasks: Set score to 0 at the very start — before the first question.
Add at least FIVE questions, each with its own check.
Vary the question types: numbers, words, and one trick question.
Test: answer everything correctly and check the score is exactly 5.
stages.check: Five questions each score correctly and the total is right.

stages.title: Grade the player
stages.goal: Give a meaningful result, not just a number.
tasks: At the end, compare the score with thresholds using '>'.
Over 4: 'Excellent!'  Over 2: 'Good work.'  Otherwise: 'Practise and try again.'
Show the score out of the total, not just the raw number.
Test: deliberately score high, medium and low, and check each message.
stages.check: The quiz gives a different, sensible message for high, medium and low scores.

stages.title: Win and lose
stages.goal: Give the game clear endings, so the player always knows how they did.
tasks: Write your rules in plain English first: 'You win when ...' and 'You lose when ...'.
Add the win check: the score is above your pass mark
Add the lose check: the score is below the pass mark
Say a message FIRST, wait 2 seconds, and only THEN use 'stop all'.
Switch to a win or lose backdrop so the ending is obvious.
Test BOTH endings deliberately — do not assume they work.
stages.check: You have triggered the win ending and the lose ending on purpose, and both work.

stages.title: Feedback and polish
stages.goal: Make every action feel good. This is what separates a finished game from a demo.
tasks: Add a sound to every important action (collect, hit, win, lose).
Add a visual effect for one action — a grow, a fade or a colour flash.
Show the score and any other variables the player needs.
Hide any variables the player does not need to see.
Test: play for 30 seconds. Can you tell what is happening without anyone explaining?
stages.check: Every action gives the player sound or visual feedback.

stages.title: Make it yours
stages.goal: Add something nobody told you to add. This is the part you will want to show people.
tasks: Use a list so questions are asked in a random order.
Accept two different spellings as correct.
Change the numbers until the difficulty feels right to YOU.
Ask someone else to play it and watch them silently.
stages.check: Your game has at least one feature that was your own idea.

L2S44.title: Advanced debugging

blockRefs.what: Stops the whole project.
blockRefs.tip: Say your message BEFORE stopping, or nobody can read it.
uses: End the game when you win or lose
Stop everything on a game-over screen

blockRefs.what: Shows a speech bubble that stays until you change it.
blockRefs.tip: It never disappears on its own — clear it with an empty say.
uses: A permanent label above a sprite
Showing a live value while debugging
A sign that stays on screen

blockRefs.what: Pauses this script for a time.
blockRefs.tip: Use 0.1 or 0.2 for smooth animation, 1 for conversations.

explain: A **bug** is a mistake that makes a program behave differently from what you intended. Debugging is finding and fixing it — and it is most of what programmers actually do.

The method matters more than luck. First state clearly what it **should** do versus what it **does**. Then narrow the search: run a single script on its own, add a 'say' to reveal a value, or add waits to slow it down enough to watch.
Change **one** thing at a time and re-test. Changing three things and finding it works tells you nothing about which one mattered.
The computer is always doing exactly what it was told. The question is never 'why is it wrong?' but 'what did I actually tell it?'

examples.title: Reveal what the code thinks
examples.code:
forever
  say (join [score is ] (score))
end
examples.note: Making an invisible value visible often solves the bug immediately.

examples.title: Slow it down to watch
examples.code:
forever
  move 10 steps
  wait 0.5 seconds
end
examples.note: If it fails too fast to see, make it slower.

deep.why: Debugging is the single most transferable skill in programming — and it teaches persistence.
deep.real: Finding out why a torch will not switch on: batteries, bulb, or switch. You test one at a time.

vocab: Bug — a mistake that makes a program behave wrongly.
Debug — to find and fix a bug.
Test — to run code deliberately to see what happens.
objectives: I can describe what a program does wrongly.
I can find the block causing a bug.
I can fix a bug and re-test.
L2S44.hook: Say: "Every professional programmer's code is broken most of the day. Finding bugs is the actual job — and you're about to be good at it." This reframes failure permanently.
teach: Give the child a project you have broken on purpose. Ask first: what SHOULD it do, and what does it do instead? Naming the gap is step one.
Teach the three moves: (1) run it and watch closely, (2) click a single script to test it alone, (3) add a `say` to see what the code thinks is happening.
Slow it down with waits so the failure becomes visible.
Fix it, then re-run to confirm. Insist on the re-test — fixing without verifying is a habit worth preventing early.
watch: Child changes many things at once → change ONE thing, then test. Otherwise you cannot tell what worked.
Child deletes the whole script in frustration → encourage isolating instead; keep a copy first.
Child assumes the computer is wrong → the computer does exactly what it was told; find what it was told.
ask: What is a bug? → A mistake making the program behave wrongly.
What is the first thing to do? → Say what it should do versus what it does.
Why change one thing at a time? → So you know which change fixed it.
L2S44.support: Debug together, thinking aloud so the child hears your reasoning; then let them lead the next one.
L2S44.stretch: Give a project with two independent bugs and ask them to log what they tried.

rubric.mastered: Debugs systematically, one change at a time, and explains the cause.

L2S45.title: Publishing your work

explain: A project is not finished when the code works — it is finished when someone else can enjoy it without you sitting beside them.
**Instructions** need three things: the goal, the controls, and how to win. Test them on someone who has never seen the project.
**Credits** matter. If you used someone's sprite, sound or idea, say so. Attribution is basic honesty, and Scratch's remix culture depends on it.
**Safety** comes first: never put your full name, school, address or contact details in a public project.

examples.code:
Goal: collect all 10 coins before the timer runs out.
Controls: arrow keys to move, space to jump.
Win: reach the flag with all coins collected.
examples.note: Three lines, no jargon, nothing assumed.

examples.title: Credits
examples.code:
Sprites from the Scratch library. Bounce sound by [name].
Based on an idea from Code Club's Ghostbusters project.

L2S46.title: Capstone: write the spec

explain: A Level 2 capstone is a **specified** project: before coding, write one page saying what it is, how it is played, and the three features it will have.
Break it into **milestones** and build one at a time, testing each. Managing a build across several sessions is the real Level 2 skill.
Use at least three Level 2 techniques — clones, broadcasts, custom blocks, lists or physics — deliberately, because they suit the problem.
Refactor as you go. If the code becomes a tangle, move sections into well-named custom blocks so the main script reads like a plan.

examples.title: A spec
examples.code:
Title: Cave Escape
Goal: reach the exit before the air runs out
Controls: arrows to move, space to jump
Features: 1) gravity + platforms  2) cloned falling rocks  3) air timer
Win: reach the exit.  Lose: air = 0 or crushed.
examples.note: Agree this before writing any blocks.

examples.title: A readable main script
examples.code:
when green flag clicked
reset game
build level
start timer
forever
  handle input
  check collisions
end
examples.note: Every one of those is a custom block. The main script reads like the plan.

L2S48.title: Capstone: features

explain: A Level 2 capstone is a **specified** project: before coding, write one page saying what it is, how it is played, and the three features it will have.
Break it into **milestones** and build one at a time, testing each. Managing a build across several sessions is the real Level 2 skill.

Refactor as you go. If the code becomes a tangle, move sections into well-named custom blocks so the main script reads like a plan.

  handle input

move () steps.what: Moves the sprite forwards in the direction it is facing.
move () steps.tip: One step is about one dot on the screen — 10 is small, 100 is a big jump.
uses: Walk a character across the stage
Fire a bullet in the direction it faces
Step an enemy along a patrol route
Draw a line of a shape with the pen

turn right () degrees.tip: 90 is a quarter turn, 180 is half, 360 is all the way round.
uses: Turn a corner when drawing shapes
Spin a fan, wheel or coin
Aim a turret step by step
Rotate a pattern in spirograph art

turn left () degrees.tip: Turning left 90 is the same as turning right 270.
uses: Steer a car or boat left
Undo a turn made the other way

turn () degrees.what: Turns the sprite by the number of degrees you choose.
turn () degrees.tip: Small turns inside a loop make smooth spinning.
uses: Wobble a sprite back and forth
Rotate a shape a little between draws
Make a slow hand on a clock

point in direction ().what: Faces the sprite in an exact direction.
point in direction ().tip: 90 is right, -90 is left, 0 is up, 180 is down.
uses: Reset a sprite to face right at the start
Make a character face up to jump

point towards ().what: Turns the sprite so it faces another sprite or the mouse.
point towards ().tip: Put it in a forever loop to keep watching a moving target.
uses: Make an enemy chase the player
Aim a cannon at a target
Make a flower turn to follow the sun
Have a pet follow its owner

point towards [mouse-pointer].what: Makes the sprite face wherever the mouse is.
point towards [mouse-pointer].tip: Great for eyes that follow you, or a turret that aims.
uses: A turret that aims where you point
A magnifying glass that tracks the mouse
A shark that swims towards the pointer

go to x: () y: ().what: Jumps the sprite instantly to an exact spot.
go to x: () y: ().tip: x 0, y 0 is the middle of the stage.
uses: Send a sprite home at the start of a game
Respawn the player after losing a life
Place sprites exactly when setting a scene
Reset a ball to the centre after a goal

go to [random position].what: Jumps the sprite to a random spot on the stage.
go to [random position].tip: Perfect for making targets appear unpredictably.
uses: Make a target pop up somewhere new
Place stars randomly in a night sky

go to [mouse-pointer].what: Makes the sprite sit exactly on the mouse.
go to [mouse-pointer].tip: The sprite will cover your pointer — offset it if that's a problem.
uses: Make a paddle or cursor sprite
Drag-and-drop feeling for a paint brush
A net that follows your hand
A spotlight that follows the mouse
